大和本草敘

本邦遠古果方嘗百草而治
疾病者邦但閑其書而未見
其緒也果有作本草而辨物
識性者那但閲其名而来見
其書也中葉已降其書办有斯
translation:
Right side (cover/title label):

Compiled and written by Master Kaibara [Ekiken] of Haibara
Yamato Honzo (Japanese Materia Medica)
Newly collated and corrected
With supplementary records
And illustrated plates of all items
Heian [Kyoto]
In the collection of Fukushōken

Left side (opening of the preface):

Preface to the Yamato Honzo

In ancient times in our land, there were those who tasted the hundred grasses and used them to treat illness, yet their writings remained obscure and unseen, leaving no thread to follow. There were also those who composed works on materia medica to classify things and understand their natures, yet people only glimpsed the names without ever seeing the books themselves. From the middle ages onward, such writings did come to exist here—

text:
〈作在邪　惟恨窮郷〈〉生
毎遠托各山而来渇閑之已
速于近世乎嘗命本草之六
一二出為持専托飲膳食治
而不備於庶物以有事乎
博治者農圃為〈笑也吉
　　　　　　　　　　　先生嘗有喜斯學何也自謂
其為寒也屡腸善病欲保其
天年則与他異知識品物之
歌快而雄別性味之良毒以
補〈以攻之方不可不自
助也乃自弱冠把読明李時
translation:
Alas, living in a remote rural place, one laments only the poverty of one's village — to have been born here.
In recent generations, people have relied on the Bencao (Materia Medica) for its guidance on the six [categories], for the preparation and management of food, drink, and medical treatment.
Yet it is not comprehensive regarding all things of daily use, and those who have made a broad study of it, including farmers and gardeners, have laughed at this — so it is said.

The Master [Ekiken] once, when asked why he took such delight in this field of study, replied that he considered himself of a cold constitution, frequently suffering from intestinal ailments, and desiring to preserve his natural lifespan. For this reason, unlike others, he came to know and distinguish the various products [of nature] and their individual properties — whether beneficial or harmful. He understood that one cannot fail to rely on [such knowledge] to supplement one's strengths and address one's weaknesses. Thus from the time of his coming of age he took up and read the works of Li Shi-

（右ページ）
弥本草綱目及諸家本草諸
州府志群書集類、中に九有、
預此去平昔無い不蒙達引、
以来録之積、且不成編、其舊闢
共新増と複不可損也遂合
纂以為大和本草十六巻以

（左ページ）
誌于世。如茲集所由有、自序
凡例丁寧シ、又何贅乎。答乃
其博而不疵也、其約而不漏
也。読者所監也不敢囿也。夫
僕事先生于最四十年矣
茶顧其肵、以研抄経渉抄史
translation:
(Right page)
The Bencao Gangmu and the various herbals of many schools, the gazetteers of the various provinces, and a great many collected works — for a long time I had been drawing on these, accumulating excerpts, yet was unable to bring them into a finished compilation. Old materials and newly added ones piled up time and again without being organized. At last I gathered them together and compiled the Yamato Honzō in sixteen volumes,

(Left page)
to be set before the world. The circumstances that gave rise to this collection are explained in my own preface and in the detailed notes on editorial principles — what need is there to add more here? The answer is this: the work is broad yet without flaw; it is concise yet leaves nothing out. These are matters for the reader to judge; I would not presume to confine anyone's view. For my part, I have served my teacher for nearly forty years, and with devoted care have researched and copied through the classics and histories,

text:
万解和州序

羅挖百氏摘挖枡編小説筍
手抄寫刻意蒐修繃稀譚考索
巨細無遺攻一手以惰濃脈
一手以窮年雖其覿蓐暮
實乃如學し挌誡鳴呼
先生し業所謂勤矣以覧観

之如其名物の学信挌物
一方兩支一件以覗或
認其一方業則安知先生し業
生し大戎斯乃吾曹不可以無
言也幸奉具命以護為之飲
translation:
Preface to the Yamato Honzo

Gathering from hundreds of scholars, selecting and compiling minor writings and treatises, copying by hand and carving woodblocks, earnestly collecting and revising, consulting rare accounts and records — leaving out nothing great or small, devoting one hand to diligently tracing the veins and threads of things, and the other to exhausting years of labor; although one may see the results only in one's late years, this is truly what it means to pursue learning, to investigate and admonish. Alas, the Master's work is what one would call diligent indeed — worthy of careful study and reflection.

Regarding the investigation of the names and natures of things: if one masters only one approach and one aspect, taking only one item as one's model, how can one know the full scope of the Master's work? The Master's great endeavor is something that we, his followers, cannot afford to neglect. It is my good fortune to have received his instructions, and so I take it upon myself to protect and uphold them with reverence.

右頁：
寶永戊子四月廿七日
門人　窪原　鞠謹題

左頁：
大倭本州自序
天地之道常行而不息為矣而天地別無所為只以生物為事而已矣物所以萬物生生不罷也是以六合之内無限矣然則學者明究於庶物之功亦可弘益於民用者亦弘多無限矣
博史以記事其次集物之書亦不可闕也且本州之學所以為切弊諸
道籍之所以不可以關也本州之學所以為切於民
生日用者亦有以也品物之良毒誠難測知藥人之
用捨亦宛慎擇不但多識其名而已也然則物理之
translation:
Right page:
On the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month of the Hōei Bosshi year [1708],
Disciple Kubohara Kiku, respectfully inscribed.

Left page:
Preface by the Author of Yamato Honshū [Yamato Honzō]

The way of Heaven and Earth moves constantly without ceasing, and yet Heaven and Earth do not act with deliberate purpose — they simply give life to things. This is why the ten thousand things are born and grow without end. Thus within the six directions [the whole world] there is no limit. If a scholar thoroughly investigates the functions and properties of all things, he too can broadly benefit the people in their daily uses — and those uses are likewise boundless without limit.
Historical records preserve events; collections of things [natural history works] are likewise indispensable. Moreover, the learning of our province must be urgently applied to correct shortcomings.
The texts of the Way cannot be neglected; the learning of our province is urgently relevant to the daily lives of the people.
Those things that are of use in daily life also have their place. The beneficial or toxic nature of the various products is truly difficult to gauge; in choosing or rejecting medicines, one must be careful and discerning, and it is not enough merely to know many names. Thus, in understanding the inner principles of things —

text:
學其關係亦不可寫小也夫以古昔聖人開物成務之功固至矣然天下之事物日開赤已故古所之無而今有古所不知而今知者不可勝耳且蕃夷各異亦是古來諸書物理之功到後也漸次隨時不可枚記亦盡用故書物理之功到後也漸次隨時不可无之無而今有古所不知而今知者不可勝耳且蕃夷各異亦是古來諸
家本州之述作所以勸多病好請本州有志於物理之學也尚矣
餘之日粗不能錄於本州之要言且於群籍之中系講
於本州所不收錯雜而記載之為開本邦所有而以舊開與膽
與群書所不載之品物據摹於本州以舊開與膽
見彼是相敷演几向十三百六十餘種分門折類繁
為廣闊蕃夷之所產群品之蓄殘其種分門折類繁字内
末學徒起望洋之嘆耳余名歷之材粗淺不億孟淵之
寄陋不能博引爭綜精而致詳姑隨見聞
見開之所及記其端末而已矣恐其闕誤多而
免後人之議訖然以為遺憾僭率之罪無所逃然
年両逐旋修政自然薄而不能待多
入精自狹至博亦為學之方也初學之士以此為萬一
精博之階梯則亦庶乎有小補于物理之學之萬一
大養草 刊白字
translation:
The significance of this subject is by no means small. In ancient times, the sages opened up knowledge of things and accomplished great works — their contributions were indeed immense. Yet the affairs and things of the world continue to expand day by day. There are things that did not exist in antiquity but exist now; there is knowledge unknown to the ancients that is known today — these are beyond counting. Moreover, the various foreign lands each differ, and since ancient times many books have recorded the principles of things; as time has passed, step by step, ever more has accumulated and cannot all be noted down.

The works composed by scholars of this province have long encouraged those with a mind for the study of natural principles.

What I have done in these days is roughly to collect what the major works do not record, gather scattered and miscellaneous items, and set them down — drawing on what exists in this land, opening old records, and comparing them with works from neighboring countries and the broader corpus of texts; items not found therein I have sought out and depicted, arranging them according to the categories of this work.

I observed how earlier writers elaborated and expounded upon these matters, reaching more than three hundred and sixty varieties in all, organized by category and class into an elaborate system — encompassing the products of distant foreign lands, the wealth of their accumulated specimens, all gathered within the compass of this work. Students of modest learning, looking up at this vast ocean, can only sigh with admiration. I am a man of crude and shallow ability, not possessed of the deep wisdom of a Meng Yuan; I cannot cite widely, synthesize with precision, or achieve thoroughness of detail. I have simply followed what I have seen and heard, recording the outlines of things as best I can. I fear there are many gaps and errors, yet I cannot escape the fault of presumption and recklessness. Over the years, revising gradually as I went, the work grew from narrow to broad — this too is the proper way of learning. If beginning students can find even one ten-thousandth part of benefit to the study of natural principles in this work, then perhaps it will serve as a small contribution on the ladder from the elementary to the comprehensive.

Yamato Honzo, printed edition.

Editorial Notes for Yamato Honzo

One: This book selects from among all the items recorded in the Bencao Gangmu (Honzo Komoku) those that are most essential and relevant, collects and records them. As for the detailed descriptions of the form, appearance, nature, and flavor of the various items, those are not reproduced here — for those, one should carefully study the Bencao Gangmu itself.

One: The Bencao Gangmu records no fewer than one thousand eight hundred and some items found throughout the world. Beyond those, among the many items not recorded in the Bencao Gangmu, there are also numerous entries scattered through various other books outside that work. Over the many thousands of years since records began, rare and unusual things and strange objects have appeared here and there in various texts, and it is possible to gather and retrieve them. Can one simply omit them from the annotations to the Bencao Gangmu? Therefore, although this book draws extensively from the Bencao Gangmu in its excerpts, numbering in the hundreds and thousands —

text:
而什一而已區所以編錄於此書者凡本草所宗載而群書之所載者予有志于收載之為久矣故用心涉獵龐雜多歷年所隨予所聞見採擇而輯錄之以備觀覧而已惟事近年所碎言類乎怪誕則舍之以涉獵而已觀聴民俗所稱品之所在本粗記當所親觀且中草木依俗稱考之以助初學之人待後涯群書而欲令姑稽考所希書則初學之人不知品物之名稱形狀群籍涉獵然則乎有小補於民用之萬一關功勞也考索於群籍浩瀚難速閱如斯書可謂其捷徑而省

自神農本經後歴代諸士所輯凡名本草者多矣
如此書因草拙隨且書之以國字不可比雖於古人之作然固記草木蟲魚禽獸之品目假僧名稱而號大和本草而已

translation:
And that is all — as for what I have compiled and recorded in this book: since long ago I have had the ambition to collect everything recorded in the foundational materia medica texts and in the broad body of writings. Therefore I applied my mind, browsing widely through a vast and varied collection, and over many years, following what I heard and saw, I selected and edited it together in order to provide a reference for reading. I have set aside only those recent accounts that seem close to bizarre fabrications, keeping only what I gathered from observation. I personally observed local common names and the locations of plants and grasses, recording them roughly as I encountered them, using vernacular names, in order to assist beginners. Those who wait for later scholars or hope to consult vast libraries — beginners will not know the names, appearance, and form of the various things. Browsing through many writings is difficult and slow. A book like this can be said to offer a shortcut and save effort, which is its contribution and merit.

Since the Divine Husbandman's Classic of Materia Medica, all the scholars of successive generations who compiled works under the name "honzō" (materia medica) have been many indeed.
A work like this, crudely written, recording grasses, trees, insects, fish, birds, and beasts — their categories and names — using vernacular names, is entitled Yamato Honzō, and that is all.

One: I have not used Chinese characters throughout. As for why — my abilities are limited and my literary skill is poor; I feared I could not write in formal prose about the relationships among medicinal substances and things, and that scholars would easily find fault.

One: Following the example of earlier writers who left records for readers, I have roughly gathered and classified items and placed them at the head of the volumes as an introduction, explaining them in plain popular language so that readers may grasp the essentials, and that is all.

大倭本草凡例
translation:
For every item found in the Chinese pharmacopoeial literature that is collected and recorded, we note it with an additional character. For items not found in Chinese texts but known in Japan by their Chinese name, those that came from southern foreign lands are marked with the two characters "barbarian variety." If something is recorded in the pharmacopoeia but is now no longer found or seen, it is left open as a new entry.

For items not recorded in the pharmacopoeia but produced in the various provinces of Japan, their names vary according to local dialect; common names used across all regions are rare. In this book, Japanese vernacular names also often reflect regional dialects, and readers should not be surprised if the names listed here differ and make it difficult to identify a species by its appearance.

Regarding ancient Japanese texts which contain erroneous character readings and mistaken glosses — one should simply examine the true form and appearance of the thing in question to determine what it is. Texts of the present day commonly call things by the names of other creatures — characters for such fish as the lu, li, tai, katsu, and for crustaceans, shrimp, crab, and plants such as tsuki, Lycoris, knotweed, maple, and polypody fern — all bearing glosses that are erroneous. In composing this work, the author has aimed to correct such old popular errors and substitute correct characters and correct readings; where no correct character exists, the common character is provisionally used.

The Japanese books relied upon include the Nihon Shoki, Man'yōshū, Engi-shiki, the glosses in the Ruijushō, and others.

The Teikinkōrai, Setsuyōshū, and Shūgakushū record characters that have been in use from the medieval period onward, but their texts contain many errors and unsubstantiated terms, particularly in the transmission of readings, and those who rely on these works as authoritative have often perpetuated mistakes. There are certainly ancient Japanese names that have been preserved without corruption, but in later times many erroneous readings of Chinese terms crept in, so that today it is difficult to use these books alone to verify correct characters; there are many cases where readers have been misled into accepting wrong characters as standard. Things have often been handed down in a mixed state of merit and error. Since antiquity, popular practice has relied on old sayings and the works of the ancients, and while it is easy to do what the ancients did, one must not follow convention blindly without examining whether the ancients exercised careful discrimination in their choices. Nor should one lightly criticize those who came before simply because their works contain errors. The Honchō Shokkan records in detail the foods of our country, their forms, properties, methods of preparation, and so forth, and consulting that work broadly opens one's understanding and is of benefit to everyday use; I have therefore also taken care to examine it thoroughly. translation:
The world has few works that deserve to be called essential guides to food and drink for our country — this book is not to be discarded. Inaka Jakusui was a native of the capital Heianjo. He was broadly versed in the materia medica texts, carefully examined many books, and was thorough and precise in treating the products of our land. Among those who have discussed things native to Japan since ancient times, many are excellent, and few have surpassed him. Therefore this book draws upon his explanations, presenting them as a contribution for all scholars.

To pass off another person's words as one's own, claiming them as one's own view — that is the behavior of a petty person. The ancients, when citing the writings of others, regularly recorded their names and cited their works. Accordingly, this book, when borrowing from other texts, regularly names those texts and their authors. The opening volume of the ancients' books would set this out — to learn without this would lead one astray; there are many books cited within this work that could be enumerated, but to list each item under each entry would be trivial pedantry and contrary to the goal of conciseness. Therefore they are not listed here.

Heaven and Earth have a heart that gives birth to all things; human beings receive that heart, and it becomes their own heart — this is what is called benevolence. The benevolent person loves all things. This principle means that a person must serve Heaven and Earth, following the principle of Heaven and Earth. To nurture and cherish people and things alike is the Way of being human, the way of serving Heaven and Earth. Mencius said: "Be affectionate toward kin, and extend benevolence to the people." There is a natural ordering of first and last, weightier and lighter — one cannot do without distinctions of degree. Extend benevolence to the people, and then love all creatures: this is the proper sequence of nurturing care. Therefore the Way of nurturing care begins with enriching human relationships. If that is so, then relieving and benefiting the people is a task that every person, in their station, ought to carry out — this is an affair close to daily life and must never be forgotten. How much more so for medicine, which exists as the art of benevolence: one must first know this principle and preserve in one's heart the mind of benevolence — this is what it means to nourish the spirit.

translation:
Yamato Honzo
Concluding General Remarks

For those who practice medicine, this is the most pressing matter, so I have placed it at the head of the volume — do not dismiss it as roundabout or irrelevant.

On the nature of things:
All people in the world are born relying on Heaven and Earth. Yet though we are human, most of us are beset by illness, and those who are comfortable and at ease, who spend their days in leisure reading books and attain long life — such fortunate people are rare. They enjoy pure blessings in abundance and cannot help but feel deep gratitude for the boundless grace of Heaven. They are set apart from ordinary people. Having first explained the meaning of the classics for beginners, yet holding no position or rank by which to render relief to the multitude, and being of no benefit as a scholar, having nothing valuable to offer externally — to go through one's whole life in this way would make one no better than a bookworm, a mere parasite in the world between Heaven and Earth, and that would indeed be a crime.

Accordingly, moved by a kind of compassion, I have from early on composed small writings in the vernacular script, producing several kinds over the years. Now I have composed the Yamato Honzo. My intention is also this: as I grow older, finding it increasingly difficult to read deeply, of modest talent and thin virtue, I do not wish to claim reputation through scholarship, nor do I shrink from the ridicule of contemporaries. The reason I have continued this work without stopping is that my purpose has always resided within myself, and that is simply how it is.

On the Medical Literature of This Province

The works that have recorded trees, birds, beasts, insects, fish, metals, jade, earth, and stones of our provinces: beginning with the Shennong Bencao, Tao Hongjing of the Liang dynasty compiled the Mingyi Bielu, supplementing the Shennong Bencao Jing, adding 365 kinds of entries. translation:
The number of items recorded in the various materia medica of Shu and Han reaches nearly 1,892 kinds. Among them, herbs are the most numerous. Song-dynasty Zheng Yuxi states: the Bencao Jing (Classic of Materia Medica) in three volumes, as well as the Annals of the Divine Farmer, are nowhere mentioned in the bibliographic treatise of the Han History, nor is there any mention of weights and measures. In the Former Han Annals, Lou Hu's name does not appear; the flavors and properties recorded are thus derived from medical formulas, which first appear in the Huainanzi. The Huainanzi says the Divine Farmer tasted the hundred medicines — the name "bencao" (materia medica) first appears in Weizong Ao's writings, placing it in the Huainanzi. Although the Huainanzi mentions the Divine Farmer tasting the hundred medicines in order to create remedies, the name "bencao" still does not appear there. The Han History, though mentioning the Divine Farmer tasting the hundred medicines, cannot determine from which era the text was composed — it is not in the Shiben or the Huainanzi. The Wangshiji states that the Yellow Emperor ordered Qibo to taste medicinal herbs and to establish the name "bencao," with Weizong noting that the Yellow Emperor is the origin of the name. This is how the various illnesses came to be treated — it is known that this province attributes the beginning to the Yellow Emperor. Chen Zangqi was a person of the Xuanzong Kaiyuan period of Tang, who compiled the Bencao Shiyi (Supplement to the Materia Medica). Lou Zhen noted that of all those who worked on the materia medica, his compilation best refined and organized the various texts, correcting the ropes of error and illuminating what earlier works had concealed — there has been no one like him since. He also said: among the names of materia medica through the successive dynasties, Chen Zangqi's identifications and clarifications of substances are the most precise. This should certainly be trusted. The successive dynasty names of materia medica and their titles are recorded in the first volume of the Bencao Gangmu.

The Wenxian Tongkao states: the name "bencao" first appears in the Han History, in the annals of Emperor Ping and in the biography of Lou Hu. The old classic comprised only one volume with 365 drug entries. Tao Hongjing added the Mingyi Bielu with an additional 365 kinds, expanding to seven volumes. During the Xianqing era, 144 more kinds were added, making twenty volumes; because of the need to verify and explain, seven more volumes were made — this is the Tang Materia Medica. The Shu version was further augmented and came to be called the Shu Bencao.

translation:
The Daguan Bencao (Grand Materia Medica) was compiled in the second year of the Daguan reign period [of the Song] by Tang Shenwei, who gathered texts from throughout successive dynasties and combined them into a work. He also drew on ancient and contemporary single-remedy texts and histories, books from a hundred schools, and appended to it all writings related to medicinal substances. In twenty-one volumes it was titled Zhenglei Bencao; the court then renamed it Daguan Bencao. From the time before the Bencao Gangmu, the complete work and the various later editions produced by numerous scholars — totaling some ten or more versions — include the work of Li Shizhen. Based on the six hundred items [in earlier editions], he surveyed the Daguan Bencao and greatly expanded and revised it, making it a meritorious contribution to later ages.

Tao Hongjing's commentary on the Bencao is considered to have explained things well, and for this reason it has been of great benefit to later generations. Zhu Xi said that Tao Hongjing, who lived as a recluse in the north and south, was not clearly identified, and that this pharmacological work was built at Jiankang in the south. The Zengroku states that Tao Hongjing excelled in compiling the Mingyi Bielu (Records of Famous Physicians).

It is said that the Bencao is a book for household use and reference, and though it cannot replace pulse diagnosis, it is trustworthy. The commentaries and investigations show that it is not merely a physician's book — it should be read by all. Its examples are most instructive to contemplate. Reading it is something of daily and urgent importance for physicians and patients alike. Those who are devoted to nurturing their health must not fail to learn from it.

Below are listed works outside the main Bencao that record things, plants, and objects — briefly noted:

Erya (with sections on birds, beasts, insects, fish, plants, and trees); Nanfang Caomu Zhuang (Plants and Trees of the South) by Guo Yigong; Qimin Yaoshu; various works on famous flowers and plants including those by Huang Shengzeng; works on rice varieties; works on seafood; texts on animals; Youhuan Jizhi; Jingyu Lu; Huashi (History of Flowers); Wang Shimao's Guashu (On Fruits and Trees); works on vegetables and melons; Gao Lian's Yeshu (Wild Vegetables).

[Section heading: Commentary and Annotations on Household Affairs]

Among works on the arts of flowers and arrangements: from the Ming dynasty, Mao Jin's works, Lu Ji's Poetic Exposition on Plants and Trees, the Essential Points on Vases of Flowers, Zhang Qiande's Treatise on Vase Flowers, Yuan Hongdao's Record of Vases; among medical works, the Bencao by Li Dongyuan, the Bencao by Li Shizhen, the Dongquan, medical Bencao texts, the Bencao for the Gate of Medicine, Liquid Bencao, the Great Bencao, also called the Bencao Jian, the Dongyi Bogam (Korean medical encyclopedia), and various others.

Under agriculture: Jia Sixie's Essential Techniques for the Common People, Duan Chengshi's Youyang Zazu, Zhu Xi's commentaries on poetry, the Nongzheng Quanshu (Complete Treatise on Agricultural Administration), the Taiping Yulan, the Tongzhi, the Tianzhong Ji, and various collected works on types of plants; the Qimin Yaoshu, the Baichuan Xuehai, the Qianjin Yaofang, the Zheng Qiao Tongzhi, and encyclopedic works of many kinds; the Xiudianzhi, medical formularies, household essential guides, and the Sancai Tuzhi.

Regarding the recording of local products of each region: outside these sources, many more references are available; the Yitongzhi (Comprehensive Gazetteer) records the birds, beasts, water creatures, fish, jade, and stones of the various provinces in great quantity, and among the southern gazetteers there is the Nanhai Zhizhi, which records in great abundance the products found throughout the southern seas.

In the early Ming dynasty, Zhou Xianwang, wishing to save the people from famine, compiled the edible plants — some four hundred and ten species — into four volumes, recording their forms and methods of cultivation. Works on cultivation methods include the Qimin Yaoshu, the Nongsang Jiyao, the Nongzheng Quanshu, the Jujia Biyong (Household Essentials), the Yueling Guangyi, the Huashi, the Huajing, the Yuanshi, and others.

translation:
There are many books on the six categories of living things — works by masters who broadly expanded upon Hua, Yulan, Denghu Yuan, Huang Sheng's writings on insects, fish, and animals — as well as works on the forms of hawks and birds, the habitats of various creatures, fish varieties, plants, birds, beasts, insects, fish, which are recorded therein. The number of such Chinese books on materia medica and related writings is beyond reckoning.

Among the Chinese materia medica works and various writings that record plants, trees, birds, beasts, insects, fish, minerals, and stones: although scholars of broad learning from ancient times are not few in number, those who have explained names and realities [i.e., matched names correctly to actual things] have time and again fallen into confusion, mixing up names and realities. The materia medica works and various writings that record things sometimes agree and sometimes contradict one another, so one cannot cling to any single account and trust it completely. As Mencius said: "To believe everything in books is worse than having no books at all." This is precisely why it is so difficult to identify things from these works.

Writers of careless books describe shapes and appearances in ways that superficially resemble one another, without clarifying differences and similarities, and use names loosely — causing readers who examine carefully to fall into error. Even this present work may well contain many careless mistakes; I can only hope that careful readers will examine and correct them.

To distinguish right from wrong through cross-referencing requires extensive study and wide observation. One must weigh doubtful matters carefully. The four errors to guard against are these: relying solely on what one has seen and heard oneself and treating whatever differs from one's own experience as wrong; being too narrow-minded, insisting only on one's own view; dismissing others by saying "I have already considered this" and moving on; and making hasty judgments based on limited and shallow experience. Anyone who falls into these four errors will certainly go astray.

(Header annotations in red, left page): Land, many stars, not [so] / Sea, established, Bun / Water, ancient, established

(Main text, right page):
The Bencao Gangmu's division of things into three grades contains many doubtful points. Chrysanthemum, mugwort, and sweet wormwood are placed among the fragrant herbs, yet though they all have aromatic qualities, they are listed under fragrant plants and the shade-dwelling herbs are not mentioned. As for the yellow earth-vine and goosefoot, the shade plants are avoided and they should not be called by that name. They are particularly different in character from the goosefoot family. In the present day people all regard them as fine vegetables and value them greatly. Yet instead of being listed as vegetable varieties, plants such as the ornamental gourd, Malabar spinach, and bitter melon — which cannot properly be called vegetables — are not included. Goosefoot is an aquatic plant and yet is listed among the shade plants. Pepper should be grouped with Forsythia as a climbing plant, yet is placed among tree fruits. It is thus wrongly described as a tree fruit; and Dichroa is grouped with the shade plants. Hence the tree fruits are recorded in error. The seeds of Dichroa stop at being classified with common mountain plants, and the flavor of fruit varieties is disregarded, being placed among non-herbal items listed under poisonous plants. Among the poisonous plants, curly dock is not an aquatic plant, yet Ranunculus is listed there. The Bencao states that when planted with stone it may be acceptable to list it under poisonous plants. Nevertheless, water parsley, which has fragrance, and saxifrage and winter cherry are placed under that category even though they are aquatic plants. Sea vegetables such as seaweed, kelp, and kombu, as well as stone callitriche and sea pine — items from the sea — are listed under this same heading, along with freshwater algae recorded miscellaneously. Although they belong to the river-and-sea category, they are recorded miscellaneously under land products. The water plant section, under dried aquatic things and sea products, lists items that are all sea vegetables and are of the same class as the aquatic plants; they belong from sea-algae onward among several types. If that is so, this is a sea-plant category, just as the fish section likewise fails to distinguish between river and sea — as in the Classic of Mountains and Seas.

translation:
The Erya and similar works all classify bamboo under herbs; there is also a theory that bamboo, being neither wood nor herb, should be placed in a separate category. Yet the Bencao Gangmu lists bamboo under the category of woody plants — a confused arrangement. The fish entries are few and incomplete. Aquatic birds such as the autumn chicken, the wren, and similar creatures are water birds, not fish; they should be classified under water birds. The distinction is difficult: scaleless fish belong among the sea creatures, yet the original classification places herons and egrets — which are not fish but water birds — alongside them. Mountain birds, likewise, are land birds. The masked palm civet and similar creatures are listed under feathered insects in the Gangmu. That creatures called "insects" are placed among birds is similarly anomalous. The entries attributed to Deng are numerous. All of the above reflects the classificatory system of Li Shizhen's Bencao Gangmu. Bats and cold-rats, being rodents, are not birds. The Dongbi Bencao's categorical divisions, or divisions by region — scholars such as Zheng have not yet resolved these matters.

This remains unexplained. Yet scholars who came from the East found that what the Bencao described could be called wildly presumptuous, and no further argument was made; later scholars accepted it without question.

To lightly criticize what the ancients did, simply accepting it without doubt, is something that later scholars of learning also could not avoid — it is one aspect of scholarly inquiry.

The rules for reading punctuation are numerous; the meanings recorded are not few, and the readings are not easy to master.

This guide to punctuation only covers so much; items not listed here were published separately in Japanese editions.

The study of natural things requires broad reading and strong memory; one must have thorough knowledge to master both ancient and modern learning.

One must reflect carefully and test things against actual specimens in order to distinguish the categories of things and understand their interrelations.

To investigate the principles of things, to correct errors, to discriminate the true from the false — this is what fellow students of learning must do.

The scope is vast and the depth is great; it is not something that a shallow, provincial student like myself, measuring the sea with a ladle or viewing the sky through a tube, can fully grasp.

I am fully aware of this; therefore, what is recorded in this book is no more than measuring the sea with a ladle or viewing the sky through a tube.

This is truly like millet grains before a great storehouse; and yet I humbly offer it in the hope that those with true ambition will make use of it.

The reason it is difficult to know plants, trees, insects, and fish fully is also due to the following: records drawn from various books are easily mixed and confused, making it hard to obtain accurate and clear distinctions. Rare and unusual things from distant regions have different names; old names become habitual corruptions that resemble yet differ from others, making clear investigation difficult. On the Principle of Things

At the beginning of creation there were no human beings; at the start of human life there was no formed change — spontaneously things came into being. What the Book of Changes calls "the qi of Heaven and Earth intermingling so that the ten thousand things are born naturally" means precisely this. The warming heat of a person's skin gives rise to insects; from stagnant water, wriggling larvae are born. From dung and soil, maggots and dung-beetles are generated; the vaporous fermentation of sea-rocks produces life; and from the earth itself...

translation:
From the moisture within, dew is produced; from leaves, tree-leaves, and fruit, insects and worms emerge. This is what is called "transformation birth" (kesshō) among the four kinds of birth. Today all such transformation birth is in fact birth through vital energy (ki). If we push the reasoning further, even the birth of male and female, of offspring from parents, is a transformation of vital essence and energy. Morphological transformation is itself fundamentally a transformation of energy. Therefore on ceremonial and fasting days the distinction between energy and form is observed. Though there appear to be two poles, if one traces each back to its source, there is but one original principle.

The viviparous (womb-born) — humans and beasts — are harbored within and emerge having nine orifices. The oviparous (egg-born) — birds and fowl — are born from within a shell and have eight orifices. The moisture-born — maggots, crickets, shrimp, and the like, as well as fish in cages and dragons in water — produce insects; they are neither womb-born nor egg-born, but come into being by following the transformations of energy. Cicadas suddenly produce lice; ants, butterflies, and wax-insects belong to this category.

As for plants in the world: the embryo of trees and grasses covers from above in the manner of womb-birth; egg-birth covers from below. Among egg-born creatures, those born on land can open and close their eggs in the sixth month; those born in moisture cannot. Moisture-born creatures spread about constantly. Transformation-born creatures pass through a stage of quiet dormancy. Clams and mussels have this stage in their eyes — they are of lesser rank among these. Womb-birth is more noble than egg-birth; egg-birth is more noble than moisture-birth. Among egg-born, those born on land are more noble than those born in moisture.

It is also said: Plants belong to the four categories of birth as follows — their skin represents moisture-birth; their fruit, growing solid and vital, represents womb-birth; [seeds in shells] represent egg-birth; fungi represent transformation-birth.

It is also said of animals: why do animals have moisture-birth? It is because their vital energy resides outside, while the inner shell houses the spirit of flowering. For plants, the head is above, rooted in the earth and drawing up toward heaven, and their bodies are warm. For plants, the root is in the earth and they ascend toward heaven; the body is warm.

The Four Births:
Womb-birth (taisei) — Egg-birth (ransei) — Moisture-birth (shissei) — Transformation-birth (kesei)

translation:
Higurashi / Tsukutsukushi (types of cicadas)
[Marginalia: "Tokkyō," "Tsukutsukushi," "cicada calls"]

(Right folio)
They dwell on the ground; their bodies are cool to the touch. It is also said that wild geese follow yin and yang and move between south and north. Large fish follow the yang and ascend or descend: in spring they go upriver, and in autumn they go downriver. Snakes and frogs follow yin and yang in going in and coming out: from spring and summer they emerge, and in winter and autumn they hide in the earth. It is also said that deep-sea fish such as the shark store eggs in the belly; the sea-chicken fish also does not open the belly — it carries the egg and gives birth. Among birds, the sparrow and all the hundred birds listen through their eggs [i.e., incubate by sound]; the snake does not forget. The duckweed floats on clear water at noon like fish-eyes, like threads without roots. The snake hears with its eyes. The cicada has no mouth yet cries. The dragon and flood-dragon can fly yet have no wings. Mandarin ducks walk in pairs; fish have no ears yet perceive. The flying horse charges and leads with its hind legs first, then its forelegs; the dragon and flood-dragon can fly without wings and travel without feet, leading always with the forelegs.

(Left folio)
There are cases of the non-sentient transforming into the sentient — for example, rocks and mountain snails transforming into butterflies, and lilies [transforming]; there are also cases of the non-sentient transforming into the sentient, such as rotting grass turning into fireflies, and putrid flesh producing [creatures of] courage and compassion. Those that fight battles and produce eggs, those that develop and give birth to live young, those without horns have fat [lard], those with prior-front [movement], those with horns have fat [suet]. Furthermore: those that eat but do not drink — the one-legged creature [kui]; those that move forward by going backwards — the centipede; those that spin as they go — the dragonfly; those that eat — [the dragonfly again].
Among [the insects]: those that sound from the flank cry out, startling and spreading their wings.
The pine-cicada sounds from its thighs; the榮原 [another cicada type] sounds from its belly.

All insects: when spring arrives they sprout buds, in summer they spread along branches, in autumn they wipe away leaves [leaves fall], and in winter [they hide and] fruits ripen. This is the constant principle by which they follow the rhythms of yin and yang — growth, flourishing, harvest, and storage.

translation:
(Right page)
Trees whose leaves are hard and thick do not shed them in autumn and winter, retaining leaves year-round. Grasses too mostly sprout in spring and live through summer, autumn, and winter. Those that sprout in summer and wither in winter follow the ordinary pattern. In Shu province, the begonia does not bloom in spring.
The calyx, buds, and such plants as various bamboos, plantains, lotus roots, and small and large reeds sprout in autumn and wither in summer.
Plants that wither in summer — narcissus and the like — are born when yang energy grows; plants born when yin energy kills — these too exist. Within one year, across the four seasons, most flowers bloom in spring and autumn, with more appearing one after another in summer and autumn as well. Plants that bloom when everything is being cut down by the killing energy, or when yang energy is growing and spring flowers bloom most abundantly, continue in succession through summer and autumn — such grasses and trees as these.

Flowers of winter: only the plum, camellia, red-berried firethorn, cold-weather chrysanthemum, loquat, narcissus, and citrus belong to this group.
Spring flowers and the like are those that bloom through autumn and winter. It is their nature to open even amid rain and snow, when the three hundred grasses of the world have all withered — these flowers bloom at that very time, amid severe winter frost and dew when every herb has dried and shriveled.

Alone in full beauty amid the grove — as the hermit Lin Hejing's poem on plum blossoms says: "While the host of fragrances shakes and falls, this one blooms alone amid the hundred withered herbs."

So it is said (in other words):

Among all grasses and trees, most grains and fruits ripen in autumn; some ripen and go on to ripen through winter — citrus, mandarin orange, and their kin are examples. Some ripen in summer: cherries, coconuts, loquats. Kidney beans, small and large eggplants, gourds, strawberries and the like ripen in summer only. There are also things that ripen in spring alone.
The natures of medicinal plants all differ from one another; leaves sprout and are shed in their own cycles through the seasons, each according to its own nature — this is the principle of nature itself. The Record of Learning says: "Great timing is never uniform."

That saying refers precisely to this.

(Left page)
Trees grow tall in summer and bear fruit in autumn; those that wither in autumn and winter follow the ordinary pattern. Likewise, those that wither in winter sprout again in spring.

translation:
In general, most flowers have five petals; six-petaled and four-petaled ones are fewer, and two-petaled ones are rare. Among five-petaled flowers, those that bloom with six petals have fruits whose kernels contain two seeds paired together. Hydrangea (紫陽花) and forsythia (連翹花) bloom with four petals. Beyond these, there are other flowers that also bloom with four petals. The flower of saxifrage (虎耳草), and the flowers of clematis (靈仙), daylily (鹿惹), and iris (射干), after blooming, are followed by three-part structures; after the flower there is one fruit. The coverings of various fruits come after the flower. In the lotus, flower and fruit appear at the same time; plants of this kind are also numerous. Among hemp-like plants, there are some that bear fruit without flowering. In the squash family there is the fig (無花果), which also bears fruit without a visible flower. Hemp has male and female plants. Willow, hazel, pepper, pink (撫子), narcissus, and similar plants bloom, with the male bearing flowers; beets (波稜) and similar plants also belong to this category. In general, among grasses and trees there are male and female, and some undergo transformation.

[On the topic of transformation:]

Among the category of spontaneous generation: gnats arise from the transformation of noxious organisms; dragonflies emerge from clams; sandpipers arise from maggots and flies; cranes arise from the metamorphosis of children's dragonflies; hawks arise from the transformation of field mice; a certain fish arises from serpents; various creatures arise from the transformation of toads into fish; cicadas arise from creatures that live underground; oysters and fireflies arise from transformations of certain organisms; swallows transform into shellfish; the severed bodies of lizards transform into sparrows or butterflies; certain marsh birds arise from transformations; mole crickets transform into butterflies; and bats undergo similar transformations.

Rice paste becomes a spirit-form; decaying matter transforms into fireflies; old grain transforms into butterflies; rotten ash gives rise to flies.

Among the inanimate transforming into the inanimate: pine trees can turn into stone; there are stones of this kind.

Among the animate transforming into the inanimate: crabs can turn into stone; there are stones of this kind.

孖子曰虎狼之父子蜂蟻之君臣羽獺之報本雎鳩
translation:
As seen in ancient texts:

Among birds, the male is generally larger and more splendid in plumage than the female; only in hawks is the female larger than the male — this is the reverse of humans, where men are strong and women gentle. The eel and the crab shed their shells and then grow new feathers and fur; for birds, feathers and fur develop inside the egg. In all birds, the taste organs develop outside the belly.

The Kinkyō (Classic of Birds) says: Mountain birds have many short tails; water birds have many long tails. Mountain birds include hawks and eagles. It also says: Birds that eat the five grains all have short beaks and short tails; birds skilled at seizing and fighting have sharp, elongated tails.

Birds that live in the mountains have short beaks and long tails; birds that live in the open fields have sharp elongated tails.

Birds that dwell on the ground and in the forest do not fly at night; they sing in the morning. Water birds hatch from eggs submerged [in nests near water].

Birds with long beaks and short tails — even if the tail seems to catch the beak — fly also at night; their calls at night are of a particular character, and their feet are similarly adapted. The flavor of their call is proportionate; their feet too are proportionally formed. Among fowl, the pheasant and the shu-bird raise themselves; their chicks, and also those of the female, belong to this category. Swallows and sparrows are of another type.

[Among birds] that breed throughout all four seasons, the chicken lays eggs month by month; the chicken sits and produces offspring throughout all four seasons; the heron produces offspring day by day.

Humans belong to the Yang, while birds, beasts, insects, and fish belong to the Yin. Yang numbers stop at nine; Yin numbers include creatures with two legs such as the heron, those with forty tails, things with eight tails, and so on.

The shōyō (a one-legged bird) has two legs; the heron has forty tail [feathers]; the horse-dragon has a hundred legs.

Master Kong said: The tiger and wolf [exemplify] the bond of parent and child; the bee and ant [exemplify] the bond of lord and retainer; the otter [exemplifies] the repayment of origins [filial gratitude]; the osprey [exemplifies loyal devotion].

translation:
Where there are distinctions, the form and vital force are biased, yet the principles of moral rightness are preserved. Yang Yongxiu said: the black-breasted crow with its cries embodies the virtue of parent and child; the honeybee's comb and the ant's nest embody the righteousness of ruler and minister; the male and female mandarin ducks embody the affection of husband and wife. The wild ducks flying in formation embody the friendship of brothers. I now consider that pelicans, male and female, share the sentiment of friends.

The heron stations itself where other creatures grow numerous, and through this surpasses them greatly. The ability to guard the night by scent is likewise a place where its superiority lies; it can thereby obtain food and benefit its companions. In all these cases, each creature's nature has a bias toward certain strengths, by which it may harmonize with its fellows.

Climbing plants all coil to the left — they follow the leftward rotation of Heaven. Above, Heaven rotates to the left. Things that fall to the right are all left-rotating; following the rule, they rotate leftward. The sun, moon, and stars all move from east to west — this is leftward rotation. Facing south, the left is the path to the east, which is west from the sun's perspective — this is leftward rotation. Even things that appear to spiral rightward are fundamentally left-rotating, moving from right to left. Twining vines and creeping plants all rotate leftward; those that fall from right to left are right-rotating. Some say that twining plants rotate rightward — this is incorrect. One should think carefully about this. Consider the interplay of vapors, white steam, and twining vines to understand their rotation.

The natures of plants and trees each differ. There are appropriate times for planting according to the seasons of Heaven — the twelve months of spring, summer, autumn, and winter each have their suitable planting times; one should plant in accordance with the seasons. There are soils of yellow and black earth, soft sandy soils, shaded grounds, sunny grounds, wetlands near ant-mounds and water margins, with or without open space — and all respond favorably to the application of manure and fertilizer.

translation:
There is bad [qi], and the treasures of the earth, when planted in proper order, are what the Classic of Filial Piety calls "making use of the Way of Heaven and the benefits of the earth." This is the method of planting trees in provinces — one must understand it.

The book Huangji Jingshi says: "When Heaven and Earth open, those born of upright qi are few, while those born of abundant qi are many. This is why humans give birth to one child at a time, while animals give birth to two or three, birds twice that, and insects twice again." This is the natural principle of things.

Again it says: "Water creatures die when they leave water; wind creatures die when they enter water. This shows that the yin provinces of Heaven become the firm yang of Earth. Turtles, terrapins, geese, ducks, and birds — these emerge from water. The yang provinces of Heaven become the yin-interior of Earth, one category."

Just as grasses and mushrooms, birds bright as forest herbs, and beasts like animals — the yin provinces of Heaven become the firm-yang province of Earth, one category.

The original text says: "Humans living beside rivers in their provinces naturally build structures for birds and beasts. Therefore grasses and trees have no knowledge."

Again it says: "Beasts have awareness but not as complete as humans; humans, however, lack certain knowledge."

Therefore, animals are fundamentally ordered by the earth, rising and descending by moisture, and animals draw qi while plants draw from Heaven, ascending by moisture from the earth and by the qi of Heaven, each taking from the heavens according to its nature.

Their nature is warm, drawing from the earth, taking its bodily constitution: grasses and trees all emerge in fives; peach and apricot blossoms have six petals.

The things generated by the earth have their complete number at five; therefore grasses and trees emerge in fives. Peach and apricot blossoms having six — those with double kernels can all kill people. [Coral/Shanshandai — illegible annotation]

Creation and transformation never produce anything complete; no thing is wholly perfect. What is rich in flowers will be poor in fruit; what is rich in fruit will be poor in flowers. The things Heaven and Earth produce are never wholly complete in both. Plum, cherry, sea [plant] —

[Volume One of Taiyōsatsu]

translation:
Plants such as the crabapple, Virginia creeper, camellia, tree peony, and herbaceous peony have beautiful flowers, yet their fruits are not edible. The chinaberry, nandina, narcissus, and similar plants have beautiful flowers but their fruits are of little use. As for plants like chestnuts, tangerines, and citrus—their flowers are not beautiful, yet they bear plentiful fruit for planting; the Eight Precious Things are not found among them, and they produce little.

On the marvelous workings of mutual control in the nature of things: these cannot be fathomed or known. Just as a magnet attracts iron, and amber attracts dust, so rehmannia and mulberry bark are incompatible with iron; grain crops are difficult to brew and cultivate together with highland barley. The properties of fermented wine likewise cannot be explained simply by the five-phase theory of conquest and generation. The way in which things control one another originates in their own nature. The nature of bears, for example, cannot be subdued by an iron cage; this is why great physical strength exists in them. As for the vacuous theory that one can pacify the hearts of the people through the liver—this is a shallow argument. Those who combine iron to repel such forces do not understand this.

The felling of trees is false learning. Someone asked: what medicines are used to treat stagnation of the liver? Those who use iron and similar means to drive away such forces do not understand the principle that all things by their nature inherently contain the logic of mutual control and subjugation. The ten-thousand-things are as one in this.

The unfolding of heaven and earth cannot be explained by reasoning that goes beyond principles. One view holds that the opening and renewal of heaven and earth transcends ordinary reason. Yet how can one say that what seems beyond reasoning cannot be examined through reason? It is not that these things are outside of principle—it is only that our investigation of principle is insufficient. Under heaven, how could there truly be anything outside of principle? It is because we know the constant but do not know the variable that we cannot exhaust the matter. This is why the investigation of principle is so prized by the gentleman. Under heaven, there is truly nothing outside of principle. This is the principle of heaven and earth.

Among grasses, trees, and bamboo, there are male and female kinds; those without fruit, though they have branches and leaves like others, are numerous—especially among bamboo. This shows that even plants have yin and yang. Among living things there are fish, which are neither birds nor beasts. Just as among plants there are grasses, trees, and bamboo—with bamboo being a separate category from trees, like what is called藏飩—so too with moving creatures.

text: 猶動物之有苔有鳥獸魚而動植各自有遣三等耳、植物類復有蟲魚而動物也最細微不可與岬木竹相比也亦動物之中有蟲最細微不可與動物類繁殖其奇珍類相比也並有介此亦動物也介植物之中有苔蘭也、南方諸靈風土中有苔草木也。往往流來于温熱故土夏暨本邦者不寒発生香木是也其餘尚為多此土。番薯鳳尾葛南瓜諸香木棉秈米則不然由寒之歳嚴蕭発生之氣少也。榿柑金橘八寒とよる教え凡文武ハ京都ヲ寒土ト云以条南五上ヲ信。北土及信州ニ橘類ナシ柚ハ山中ニモアリ橘相ハ朝鮮ニ寒地三安乙故三紀州駿州肥後ニ多し也舊鳳尾蕃薯等寒地之故二橘相ノ類及茶ナレト此北土及信濃甚國六ナニ茶八山中三毛亦有之候レ尾近江美濃ヨリ寒ク故前ノ駿賀ニツカハシ奥州羽州ニ六畿内諸州ニ實ル茶モ北州ニハトリ信州岐岨ノ谷中ニ八竹ナシ楢ノ小枝ヲ以テ插ノ籬トス竹簀スベテナシ中華ニモ南方ノ閩中ニ八荔枝龍眼佛手柑橄欖甘蔗等アリ
translation:
Just as plants have mosses, and animals have birds, beasts, and fish, so too among the myriad living things each category has its own three ranks. Among plants there are likewise insects and fish, and these belong to the animal category; the smallest and most minute cannot be compared to trees and bamboo. Among animals there are also insects, the most minute and subtle, which likewise cannot be compared with the category of繁殖 rare and precious things; alongside these there are shellfish, which also belong to the animal category. Among plants there are mosses and orchids. In the southern regions, various spiritual winds and soils produce mosses and vegetation. Fragrant woods and the like flow in from warm climates and survive the summer heat; in our country those that cannot endure cold germinate in seasons of warmth — such are aromatic woods. Sweet potato, fern, arrowroot, pumpkin, various fragrant woods, cotton, and indica rice are not like this; in cold years when the cold is severe, the vital energy for germination is diminished.

Regarding citrus fruits, kumquats, and hardy oranges: Kyoto is counted as cold soil; in the northern provinces and Shinano there are no citrus trees; yuzu, however, grows even in mountain valleys. The Citrus group is found in Korea as well as cold regions. Tea therefore grows in places like Kii, Suruga, and Higo in great abundance; the old fern and sweet potato varieties are also suited to cold regions. Citrus and tea are found in mountain districts from Kii through Omi and Mino; but farther north, in Ōshū and Uzen, and in the Kinai provinces, tea can be cultivated. In Shinano and the gorges of Kiso there is no bamboo; hedges are made by inserting small branches of oak, and there is no bamboo matting at all. In China too, in the Fujian region of the south, there are lychees, longans, Buddha's hand citrons, olives, sugarcane, and the like.

translation:
The Eight Absences of These Species in the Right Region

The Rites of Zhou, Artificers' Records states: "The mandarin orange crosses the Huai River northward and becomes the trifoliate orange; the myna bird does not cross the Ji River; the wild boar route, if submerged, leads to death." This is the influence of local climate and conditions. Considering that the southern regions have medicinal fish, yet the northern seas do not produce them; the northern provinces produce sea bass with large mouths; the Hakone mountains mark the eastern and northern boundary beyond which certain species do not occur; the western provinces have no white geese, and Oshu has the purple snipe, while cranes are not found in other provinces; in Hizen province and the five Rikudo islands there are foxes and raccoon dogs, while in Shinano and the Hokuriku Road provinces these species are not produced.

In Japan, compared with China, spring thunder does not penetrate to allow cattle and horses through certain regions. The rest of the details regarding which things are produced or not produced in the various widely spread provinces, whether in the south, north, east, or west — their principles are as follows: the reason why, across the vast four seas, the various regions differ in what they produce or do not produce is that there are natural distinctions under Heaven.

In general, trees, birds, beasts, insects, fish, and shellfish all vary according to region in whether they exist or not. Therefore, what China produces, our country does not produce, and what our country produces varies among provinces. The types of fish, shellfish, and insects are many and varied; to exhaustively know the presence or absence throughout Japan's provinces is difficult. How much more so for the interior of Shandong province — it is impossible to peer into every detail. The encyclopedic Convenient Reference to Classics states: Shandong has no tigers, Zhejiang has no wolves, Guangdong has no hares, Sichuan has no cranes; also, east of the Yangtze produces no foxes. The Youyang Zazu notes that Shu Commandery...

translation:
The Bencao (Materia Medica) by Li Shizhen states: among trees there are herbs, and among herbs there are trees — this is something that is neither tree nor herb.
In the regions south of Zhuti there are no cranes or magpies.
[Note: three-feathered type — said to resemble the rose and Indian lotus varieties]
Among grasses: Huacai (colored herbs), Yanghua (willow catkins), flower buds, mid-spring flowering plants, forsythia and similar types; among trees: wolfberry from Zhouzhi county.
In China and among the various foreign peoples, people ate liver as military provisions; this was the practice during the time of the Han armies.
The Vermilion Bird too was said to be favored food; those who ate it were many — this was during the time of Emperor Yin.
People of central China did not find repulsive insects, snakes, frogs, and things collected in pans, basins, and from anthills, with their urine-like stench.
The taste is said to be fine; when illness strikes, various insect remedies are used.
Outside, Song Zhu or similar texts say it can be read and heard that people in Bangu eat snakes in Hunan and Huguang.
It is said to be used both externally and taken internally. In Japan, there are surprisingly similar things.
People eat large earthworms and large salmon; people of Guangnan eat river fish; in markets, people are surprised by those who eat snakes, worms, and maggots — yet they do not find these dishes unacceptable.
There are many more such examples. In our country (Japan), even when military provisions run out in camp, people do not resort to such things — or so it is said.
When people are driven by hunger and eat, they say fish and birds taste wonderful.
Japan is a rich and fertile land, blessed by nature. Perhaps this is due to the nature of its climate and soil? Or perhaps it is said:
Many polluted and unclean things are not eaten; unlike other countries where meat-eating is common, perhaps this is the reason.
For various fish, the quality varies with the four seasons, with good and bad flavors, strong and mild tastes. The sea bass tastes best in the sixth and seventh months, and at other times is inferior. The winter carp tastes best in winter.
The flatfish tastes best in winter; in summer months the flavor is plain. The sea bass is best in winter.

translation:
The flavor of fish in spring is good. The cuttlefish is good in summer. The crucian carp is best in the second, third, and fourth months. In winter its flesh is thick and its flavor is rich. As for other fish in general, their quality — good or poor — varies according to the season. The flesh of birds and beasts likewise has good and bad qualities depending on the season. This is because all living creatures flourish or decline according to the season, and their flesh becomes fat or lean accordingly.

Manshin [a source] records that when Zhou Lianzhen visited the local gazetteer of that province, he noted that among the plants, trees, birds, beasts, and fish there, some are the same as those in China, but many others whose names he could not identify. Among things seen in the water, there were flowers of many varieties, likewise unknown by name — things never before seen in China.

Manshin also writes: in Tango, and in the Gazetteer of Da Yu, it is recorded that the products of the southern regions are also exceedingly numerous. The writings on regional products state that the Gazetteer of the Central Plains and the Gazetteer of Da Yu together cannot compare — the things produced between heaven and earth, and the dragon's domain, are also vast. The rare and extraordinary things of the east are innumerable, and the extraordinary products of any single country alone are without limit. If what is produced in just one region is already like this, how much more so across the breadth of the four seas, so vast and boundless — the extraordinary products are immeasurable. Thus it is truly difficult to seek to fully know and identify all things.

As for geese, wild ducks, and other waterfowl — all large and small birds of this kind come in autumn and return north in spring. As to where they spend the summer, I have not found this recorded in any of the many books I have consulted. However, in both Japan and China, wild cranes and similar birds all return north in spring, so their summer dwelling must be in the far northern lands. Accordingly, I have heard that in the regions of Upper Ezo and Lower Ezo, in summer the geese and wild ducks are very numerous, and it is said their feathers fall out at that time. In general, of the large and small birds that migrate back and forth from the northern lands, perhaps seven or eight out of ten make the journey, while those that remain constantly in this land are few.

translation:
Thus the places it comes and goes are not limited to Ezo; throughout China, Japan, and the northern regions of India,
as well as various foreign countries,
the crucian carp of Huálè in China, the carp of Dongting Lake,
and in our land the crucian carp of Ōmi, the carp of Yodo, the sea bream of Echigo, the abalone of Noto, Suō, and Oki — these are all famous regional products.
Master Ji Quan said: Among vegetables, the finest to eat are those washed with their roots and leaves still attached; nothing surpasses garden-grown greens watered with fertilizer.
However, many of these are washed in ways one would not wish to know about. The person washing the vegetables merely sloshes them about in water, moving them left and right in muddy water, picking and eating them without properly cleaning them. Once the task is done, one thinks the job is finished. Yet as anyone who knows would understand, what is visibly soiled can be removed, but what has dried on is hard to remove — and over months and years the accumulation of filth silently invites harm.
To achieve proper washing, one should imitate the method of washing a Buddhist statue: washing requires care and must be done by a diligent person. An impatient person washing vegetables will simply dip them in water and scrape them hastily.
To make dirt come off easily, use a brush when washing vegetables — the brush can reach high and low, around curves and bends, into every nook, and only then can the vegetables be truly clean at their core, after which seasoning can be added and the full effort of preparation completed.
The Shijing commentary of Yuan says: The ancients did not use garden vegetables in ritual offerings; in those years they dried them over firewood fire.
Lotus leaves and other plants were used frequently as mulch in the ceremonial fields, and no manure was used — only fragrant water for rinsing.
The method for washing away the grime from clothing requires attentive and careful attention, as Master Li Quan's explanation, An Wu, says.
These are things common custom has never spoken of, yet they are matters where human effort can make a full difference. The Zuozhuan says: "Prominent weeds..."

translation:
The "Records of the Grand Historian" (Shiji), in the "Biographies of Merchants" chapter, says that planting trees is profitable; the ghost-spirit [ritual use] says it is also because of their purity. Likewise, the aquatic greens offered at spirit shrines are chosen for their purity.
Chestnuts: in Shu (Sichuan) and Han, the Jiangling region had a thousand trees of orange; north of the Huai River, a thousand trees of osmanthus; the Bamboo region had a thousand mu; in Chen and Xia, a thousand mu of mugwort; in Qi and Lu, a thousand mu of mulberry and hemp; in the Wei River valley, the equivalent of a thousand-household lord, and so on. Now, according to the historian's records, all these are said to be mugwort — they are all planted as beneficial things. In our country, things planted for the people's benefit include tea, citrus, and lacquer.
What are called "beneficial plants" — in our country, those planted for the people's use include tea, citrus, and lacquer.
Among trees: paulownia, Chinese parasol tree (used for timber), peach, apricot, chestnut, jujube, orange, kumquat, tea, citrus, lacquer, mulberry, hackberry, chinquapin, camellia, zelkova, bitter orange, rattan, camphor, torreya, various species, Japanese pepper, gardenia, pear, hazel, Japanese cedar-type, tung oil tree.
Cedar, elm, mulberry, rakan pine, and bamboo varieties; grasses that are worth planting are many.
All of the above — chestnuts, citrus, catalpa, lacquer, mulberry, bamboo — every one of these can also be cultivated in Japan.

In Japan, things that did not exist in ancient times but came later from China and foreign countries include: sheep, pigs, cranes, egrets; orange, chrysanthemum, narcissus, bodhi tree, various grains; western jasmine, sugar, glutinous rice, tea, tobacco, chili pepper, cotton, autumn-flowering plants; luffa, watermelon, banana, sweet potato, plum, cockscomb, morning glory, sugarcane; and countless others too numerous to record. Among these, glutinous rice and cotton are especially beneficial to the people and nothing else compares to them.

Kunlun is likened to the ridgepole at the center of the four directions. In the four directions lie the various lands with differing climates. The central plains (China), Japan, and Korea all lie to the east of the center, and therefore their climates and soils share certain characteristics.

translation:
The human form, along with three shared categories of manufactured goods, are largely alike in their general structure; the rest that exist in the south are similar as well.
The forms of birds, beasts, plants, and trees are also the same; manufactured goods are also largely similar in their general construction. The remainder found in the south are also similar.
As for the Western regions, the land, climate, and customs are each different; humans and manufactured goods are also unlike, and vessels and implements differ as well.
In one country many languages, customs, and practices differ, though in one direction.
In another country, humans, plants, and trees — not only these but also vessels and clothing — share a similar character.
In foreign lands, humans and plants are shaped like those of the Red Barbarians [Dutch/Europeans]; hence the vessels, clothing, and structures of those lands are also different.
Manufactured goods are also unlike; the Red Barbarians' cattle-like forms come to this country in many things; their coloring is quite unlike, and their shapes differ.
Again, in Japan, the varieties from China differ; even those of the Red Barbarians differ in form.
It is thus to be known that the materia medica recorded here also differ from both Japanese and Chinese sources.

Ox Bezoar
Bezoar is found inside the body of an ox. Fish gallstones are found in the bellies of oxen, horses, and various beasts.
The precious concretion is found in dogs. The Wen Xin Diao Long states it is found in the body of the monkey. Pearls are found in shellfish.
Similarly, disease concentrates in these, accumulating within the heart and belly, taking a human-like form.
It arises in illnesses; even under heat, its essential spirit and vital fluid
congeal at certain points, or become fixed and stagnant due to pathogenic qi.
The Yishu Daquan, chapter 19, notes that pathogenic stagnation — the material so described — is a rounded precious concretion associated with epilepsy in dogs.
It is obtained from the belly; the rounded precious concretion is similarly related to chronic illness.
Plants such as turmeric (ukon), ginger, red banana, taro, and similar kinds are all good against cold.
When left in the garden in winter, their roots all rot and die; if buried in a warm, sun-facing place, they will survive.

translation:
As for plants growing in the warm southern regions, if one transplants them into gardens here, they do not die — this is due to the virtue of the local climate.

In the present age, according to the tastes and fashions of ordinary people, the forms and appearances of plants and trees have proliferated endlessly in countless variations. This is entirely dependent on what people admire and prize, and does not borrow the power of nature's own transformation. Among herbaceous plants, those that show the greatest variety of changed forms and colors include: tree peony, peony, chrysanthemum, rose, orchid, autumn flowers, carnation (stone bamboo), balloon flower, lily, morning glory, spring radish, hollyhock, cockscomb, garden balsam; and among trees: plum, peach, cherry, camellia, spring tea-plum, and azalea.
Among plants and trees with pungent flavor, the flowers of certain Kyushu trees appear in three transformed forms, with many varieties of color.

Pungent herbs and trees include:
Radish root, watercress, ginger, pepper, Japanese pepper (sansho), cinnamon, Japanese pepper-tree (藤天蓼), wasabi, cubeb pepper (朴子), and other such varieties — in all, ninety-one herbs and eleven types in total.

All pungent things remove stagnant qi, disperse food accumulation, eliminate worm accumulations, disperse cold qi, and relieve pestilential conditions.

Those who are unlearned do not apply themselves to the study of plants, trees, birds, beasts, and fish. Even among Confucian physicians in Japan who are fairly well-read, many do not pay careful attention to learning about native plants, animals, and fish. Similarly, among learned men in China and Korea, there are those who, though versed in literature, are ashamed of their ignorance of plant and animal names, and cover it up rather than seeking true knowledge. People of various lands who do not know the names of plants and trees are ashamed of the fact, yet try to bluff their way through rather than truly mastering the subject.

[Left page — On transplanting trees and plants]
In general, when transplanting trees and plants, one must understand the proper timing and conditions for each species according to its nature, taking into account the soil and climate.

Different species vary: mountain plants have three kinds of conditions; northern cold and warm climates differ in their conditions and timing; sandy-soil plants, if planted at the wrong time, will not grow, or may wither and die without taking root. The same applies to transplanting — timing relative to the plant's condition is essential.

It is said: when a spring-leafing tree is in full leaf growth in spring, or after autumn leaves have fallen in the ninth or tenth month, it may be planted. For leafed trees, four to five months after the spring leaves have come out is acceptable. In general, spring is the best time; the first through third months are the optimal period, with the later months being second-best.

A gardening text states: The best time to plant trees is the first month; the second and third months are middling; later times are inferior. One must settle the root-ball well so as not to damage the roots. Another passage states: There is no fixed time for planting trees — do not let the tree "know" it is being moved; this means to settle the root-ball firmly without injuring the roots.

Simaguong's Dule Yuan Ji (The Garden of Solitary Pleasure) records various herbs and identifies them by name and appearance, but he did not pick them.

Yamato Honzō, Volume 2
On the Use of Medicines

Medicines have five flavors, four qi, seven interactions, seven formulas, and ten categories; they have the roles of sovereign, minister, assistant, and courier; they ascend, descend, float, and sink. There are prohibitions on taking medicines, prohibitions for pregnancy, and dietary prohibitions — all of which are set forth in the Introductory Section of the Bencao. Li Dongyuan's examples of matching medicines to symptoms, and various other explanations, are all recorded in the Introductory Section of the Bencao, and are thorough: one must read them carefully.
The Yixue Rumen and the Bencao Mengquan summarize the drug properties in verse — four-character or six-character lines organized by rhyme — covering the properties and actions of various substances fairly completely. Later scholars have also composed mnemonic verse to guide students, which may truly be called a labor of dedication.

translation:
Students must read and memorize Chen Jiamo's Bencao Mengquan; its essential points may also be drawn upon. Wang Ji, styled Shengzhi, also known as Shanshi, composed the Yidu in seven volumes, which records medicinal properties using rhyming phrases to aid memorization. It differs from the Bencao Mengquan in its treatment of medicinal properties. Being precise and well-grounded, it is certainly not appropriate to cut it apart or diminish it, as that would be of no benefit when seeking formulas to address conditions — one must gather its strengths and store them.

Li Ting said: Whether an illness worsens or improves is entirely bound up with the harmonizing and restraining [properties of medicines].

When the qi is pure, recovery comes swiftly; sometimes combining [ingredients] causes flavors to multiply and the effect to circulate, whereas using a single herb alone — as is also said: each use involves mutual assistance, support, and guidance; when combined, the assisting ingredient serves to consolidate the effect. [See] Rumen Shiqin.

Liu Wansu said: Cold, heat, warmth, and coolness — these four qi arise from Heaven. Sour, bitter, acrid, salty, sweet, and bland — these six flavors are produced from Earth. Thus, what has form gives rise to flavor; what has no form gives rise to qi.

[Heading:] Yin

Li Dongyuan said: Medicinal substances possess the warm, cool, cold, and hot yang qi of Heaven, and flavors rising and penetrating; the flavors — acrid, sweet, bland, sour, bitter, and salty — belong to Earth. Numerous flavors arise from Earth's many qualities.

Qi Bo said: Sour is not produced [from metal]; humans produce bitter; Earth produces acrid; Water produces salty. One explanation says: bland permeates, bland purges; Metal produces acrid; Water produces salty.

Acrid — its qi being bland belongs to the yin of Earth; numerous flavors multiply.

Zhang Zhihe said in his discourse to two students: What one must be careful of concerning dental ailments — also said: the five terminal [tastes] cause dispersal and do not consolidate. Sour damages the teeth; prolonged use of taro and cloud-ear fungus hardens and makes them salty. One explanation: bland permeates, bland purges. The point of this passage is that when taking medicines one must be very cautious and careful.

The Bibliographic Treatise in the Former Han History states: A person who has an illness and does not treat it will as a rule receive middling medical care. The New Tang History records Sun Simiao as saying: A person without illness should not rashly take medicines; if one keeps medicines in readiness as a provision, then store them.
