translation:
On the Imbalance of Qi

The Qianjin Fang states, and Zhang Zhongjing likewise states: the human body, when in natural harmony, requires only good nourishment and care; one must not recklessly take medicines. Medicines are inherently biased toward one direction, and when taken without need, they cause the organs' qi to become unbalanced.

It is further said: A physician must first deeply understand the origins of disease, know what has gone wrong, and treat with food first. If food therapy does not cure the illness, then medicine is prescribed afterward. But medicinal substances are fierce and violent in nature — like commanding fierce troops — and so how can one casually deploy them?

Liu Zhongda's writings state: The ancients spoke of three cases that cannot be cured, the middle of which is finding a competent physician. This is a true saying indeed. When people fall ill, they rashly put no care into selecting a physician, whether skilled or not, and day and night swallow a hundred medicines mixed together without pause, seeking rapid results — this is what is called "getting stuck in the mud." It is no way to treat illness.

Mechanically following ancient formulas is also wrong. Only by nimbly adjusting and modifying prescriptions according to circumstances — what is called adapting to change — does mastery reside. This is the tradition of the ancient physicians.

All medicines are inherently biased in their qi. Such biased qi enables them to attack and expel disease. Once the disease is gone, one must not continue taking medicines regularly. In ordinary times, one should nourish oneself only with grains, meats, vegetables, and greens. Healthy people must not take medicine. Even if a medicine is classified as superior grade, it is still inherently biased in nature, and if a healthy person takes it, it will actually end up harming them — as if attacking a healthy child with harsh, assaulting medicines.

Danxi said: Whenever I treat illness, I rely principally on the medicines of Dongyuan and apply the formulas of Zhongjing, reducing the number and variety of ingredients so that the medicinal strength becomes concentrated and refined. — From the Yijing Xiaoxue.

translation:
The Su Wen records Qi Bo as saying: When treating disease with strong poisons, eliminate eight parts in ten; when treating with non-toxic medicines, eliminate six parts in ten; when treating with medicines of ordinary toxicity, eliminate seven parts in ten. Then nourish with grains, meats, fruits, and vegetables to complete the recovery — do not exceed this, lest it harm the true qi. He also said: For those who can tolerate strong medicine, use concentrated drugs; for those who cannot tolerate strong medicine, use mild drugs. Wang Bing commented: When the qi of a drug is powerfully biased, use drugs to attack the condition, but once the illness is resolved, stop at once. Zong Shi said: In general, toxic substances should only be used to attack toxicity — if used for six, seven, eight, or nine days, stop. Zhen states: In general, toxic substances should only be used when necessary — once the disease is resolved, stop immediately. Li Shizhen states: The six atmospheric influences of Heaven — wind, cold, summer-heat, dampness, dryness, and fire — when they produce disease, it is mostly in the lower body. The six flavors of Earth — sour, bitter, sweet, pungent, salty, and bland — fog, dew, rain, snow, water, and mud — when they produce disease, it is mostly in the upper body.

On the Classification of Medicines as Ruler, Minister, Assistant, and Envoy:
Qi Bo said: That which governs the disease is the Ruler; that which assists the Ruler is the Minister; that which responds to the Minister is the Envoy. Ma's commentary states: This passage speaks only of Ruler, Minister, Assistant, and Envoy as a unified concept — it does not mean actual rulers and ministers. The Minister is what is called the Assistant; it is not a literal minister. Separately, there are the roles of Assistant and Envoy. The Introduction to Medicine states: That which governs and attacks the pathogenic influence is the Ruler; that which supports the Ruler in addressing the disease is the Minister; that which guides the medicine to the right location is the Assistant and Envoy.

Tao Hongjing said: When grinding and preparing medicines, the general rule is that roots are mostly gathered in the second and eighth months. At the beginning of spring, the moisture and vital force have just begun to stir — the branches and leaves have not yet fully developed, and the potency concentrated within is pure and strong. By autumn, the leaves have withered and the moisture has flowed back down to the roots. In general, spring gathering should be done early; autumn gathering should be done late.

translation:
Flowers, fruits, and leaves each approach their maturation at different times. It has also been said: "Physicians who do not know medicines merely listen to what market people tell them; and market people in turn cannot truly discern or investigate their quality." It has also been said: "The making and transmission of medicines in medical households — distinguishing true from false, good from bad — all depends on genuine discernment." Chen Jiamo stated: "The trading of medicines mostly takes place in the markets. Who says that medicinal ointments need both eyes? These are not empty words." To place sincere trust in this saying is essential knowledge for a physician. One must know that even today those who sell medicines cannot fully equip themselves with both eyes: they use ten-thousand-year-old goat's horn sold as dried artemisia, and add foul-smelling citrus sold as bupleurum root — such mislabelings are not few. Therefore, can those who use medicines afford not to have both eyes?

Kong Zhiyue said: "Plants and animals take form through the movements of life; they are born in spring and autumn, responding to seasonal qi — though their substance may be the same, their effects differ from what is expected if gathered [at the wrong time], for they may contain harm."

When plants are removed from their native soil, their nature and flavor become variable in medicinal use, and their warming or cooling properties frequently differ in effect.

Kou Zongshi said: "For the various herbs, insects, and creatures produced in different provinces, the roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits must be gathered according to region. The local provincial prefatory notes are of the greatest importance to a gentleman and his elders."

If not gathered from the proper locality, the nature and flavor will be somewhat altered; if not gathered at the proper time, the qi and flavor will be incomplete. Moreover, new physicians differ from one another, and vary from coarse to refined — if one uses medicines without selecting carefully, any failure in effect is the physician's own fault. The prefatory notes also say: "The good physicians of antiquity all gathered their own medicines."

It is further said: "In using medicines, one must always select according to the soil and region that suits them. Those with a reliable basis may be used — for example: ginseng from Shangdang, milkvetch from Mian, Chinese angelica from Chuanxi, rehmannia from Huaiqing, and pinellia from Qizhou."

translation:
Huazhou asarum (saishin): The same is used as medicine in Japan. One must choose the land where it is produced. In Yamashiro, the angelica (toki) and in Yamato, the phellodendron (kihada) and their kind each depend on the suitability of the land. Things produced in suitable land have good properties. Things produced in land unsuitable for them have inferior properties and poor production.

For general use: Chen Jiamo states: In all the various provinces, trees, insects, and all living things each have lands particularly suited to them. Their flavor and medicinal power naturally differ from the ordinary.

The Jukaihitsuyo states: In this province, roots gathered in the eighth month are especially poor in understanding the nature of the herb. In the eighth month, the leaves are still drying and the vital energy (ki) has not yet fully returned to the roots. In the second month, the vital energy is already concentrated in the roots. For this reason, the ancients gathered pearls and roots in the eighth and ninth months. Shen Cun-zhong in his Bitan (Dream Pool Essays) states that for leafy medicines, those whose roots are gathered in the first or eighth month are best, because in the eighth month the leaves have not yet withered.

In general, when gathering and using medicines, one must first examine their authenticity and assess their quality, distinguishing the similar from the different, then select for use. One must note that things from unsuitable regions, having inferior properties, vary in flavor — some better, some worse — just as with various foods. Unless the vital energy is complete, the leaves and vegetables cannot be used. One must take note of the region of production, for flavor varies between good and bad accordingly.

Things whose leaves are taken: harvest after the eighth month and before the twelfth month, in the morning. For roots taken from where they grow: take during summer when the leaves are at their fullest, from the place of the roots. For things whose nature is known: in the twelfth or first month, when the vital energy is fully concentrated in the roots. For things gathered before sprouting: this is considered the prime time; take before the eleventh month.

translation:
After the [appropriate] month, the roots and fruits have fully ripened. In general, flowers and leaves should be gathered at their peak bloom, fruits at their point of full ripeness, and roots when their vitality is fully concentrated in them.

For harvesting roots: it is best to collect them early in spring, or late in autumn, as these are the times when the concentrated vital energy (seiki) is densest. Leaves gathered in summer or autumn should be dried in the sun; those gathered in winter or spring should be dried in the shade. According to the Kaibao Bencao: "Roots and seedlings of grasses and trees gathered before the ninth month should be shade-dried in situ. Those gathered later should be steam-processed, or prepared with honey, wine, vinegar, or child's urine." The methods of processing — roasting, frying, toasting, braising, steaming, earth-processing, salt-processing, child's-urine processing — each suit the particular substance. These are the ingenious methods the ancients used to control and moderate the properties of substances. Some things antagonize copper, some antagonize iron — these rules must not be ignored.

One must understand these principles before establishing a preparation method. One must never transgress them. Furthermore, for substances of strong toxicity, special preparation is required. The appropriate dosage must be carefully determined according to whether the patient is an adult or child, whether the condition is exterior or interior, deficiency or excess, and whether the disease is located in the upper or lower body. The proportion of water to medicinal liquid, whether more or less concentrated, must be carefully judged. The quality of the firewood and charcoal matters as well — there are differences in their quality. For purely tonifying decoctions, a gentle flame should be used and the medicine taken in small sips slowly. This gentle fire is called a "civil fire" (bubi). For dispersing and unblocking formulas, it is appropriate to take larger doses and use a combined civil-and-martial fire.

translation:
When decocting medicine quickly, do not let it boil too long but take it frequently. A strong flame means a vigorous fire.
Those taking medicine must also consider whether the illness is located in the upper or lower body, and whether there is food stagnation or retention, and take the medicine accordingly. Moreover, the daily dosage of medicine should be carefully calibrated so that it is neither excessive nor insufficient. If this is not done properly, even well-matched treatments will show no effect. Powders disperse; decoctions wash away. For chronic illnesses, use decoctions; for acute illnesses, use powders.
Li Dongyuan said: Decoctions act gently and powders relieve and treat gradually. The Rumen says that speed cannot be achieved with illness. Pills made large should be chewed fine and the decocted juice drunk — this is the ancient method. The Rumen says that without an iron blade, one cannot cut fine. For conditions of heat, decoct finely and drink hot to dispel heat; use ginger to supplement original qi, and jujube to dispel wind-cold.
Powders are fine ground herbs. They stop and remove accumulations of qi in the stomach and intestines. For illness above the diaphragm, use honey-fine powders — these do not travel along the channels and collaterals.
The Rumen says: Powders are fine ground herbs that stop and remove accumulations of qi in the stomach and intestines. For lower-body ailments, pills should be very small, round, and smooth, so that treatment reaches the middle and lower regions. For conditions treated at the upper level, gather extremely small, finely ground pills with paste so that dissolution is slow and the effect reaches the middle and lower regions. Pills made with wine or vinegar are chosen for their astringent and concentrating effect. To remove dryness, make pills with ginger juice — the Rumen says this neutralizes toxicity. Thin paste pills are chosen because they dissolve easily. Honey-refined pills are harder to dissolve. Wax pills are chosen so that the effect is gradually and progressively released, guarding against toxic medicines damaging the spleen and stomach.

Zhang Yuansu said: For illnesses located in the head, face, and skin, medicines must be stir-fried in wine. The Rumen says this is to make the medicine ascend —

translation:
Yamato Honzo, Volume 2

When a condition rises upward — for ailments above the navel and in the throat — medicines should be soaked and washed in wine. The Nyūmon (Introductory Text) says that daily one should soak and wash in wine. For conditions located below, cold medicines must be soaked in wine to assist their dispersing action. The Nyūmon states that medicines such as daio (rhubarb), chihaku (phellodendron/anemarrhena) must necessarily be prepared with wine; soaking those that act on the lower body in wine prevents the cold nature of the medicine from damaging the stomach. The Nyūmon says that all medicines should be prepared and combined in advance; if one attempts to prepare them only when the illness occurs, many of their properties cannot be fully brought out. As a general rule: when decocting a soup, use a gentle fire and bring to a small boil. A soup meant to invigorate uses less water and takes more of the juice. A soup meant to be mild and nourishing uses more water and takes less of the juice. This follows the example of Tao Hongjing of this province.

Chen Zang's notes:
For common people, the preparation of medicines is best done in moderation. If insufficient, the therapeutic effect will not come; if excessive, problems arise. (Clear the foam first.)

Water and fire together are the bases of preparation — three methods, though many techniques exist, none departs from: wine preparation, vinegar preparation,童便 (boy's urine) preparation, salt preparation, honey preparation, and earth-wall preparation.

Wine preparation raises and lifts; boy's urine preparation removes fierce properties and directs downward; rice preparation removes dryness and harmonizes the middle; wine preparation makes medicines move to the kidneys and soften hardness.

Milk preparation moistens and nourishes, builds blood; honey preparation sweetens and supplements the original qi; old-wall earth preparation refines the true qi.

Supplementing the middle jiao: outer skin preparation suppresses harsh properties and prevents injury to the upper intestine; black soybean decoction combined with herb decoction soaks and disperses, neutralizes toxins and balances; sheep's vinegar, lard, and pig fat applied by scorching.

Salt soaking is easy for beginners; removing the pith and inner core eliminates irritation and reduces agitation.

A note for beginners: if the amount of water used when decocting is too little, the medicinal flavor will not come out; if too much, prolonged boiling wastes the medicinal strength.

The Nyūmon says: if a decoction is overdone it loses its efficacy. When decocting all medicines, avoid copper and iron vessels; it is best to use —

translation:
Regarding "descending" [medicines]: one need not insist on a single large dose; taking them in smaller amounts continuously will nourish and replenish thoroughly, while taking large doses repeatedly produces a sudden and powerful supplementing effect.

[Notes on the general use of supplementing decoctions:]

All supplementing decoctions and gold-category formulas, when water is added and consumed to exhaustion, are equal to a single dose; all of them first produce a violent supplementing action.

For people who are dry and depleted, one should generally follow this order of use as a guideline.

The Ju Fang (Bureau of Formulas) General Rules state: supplementing and tonifying medicines must be prepared correctly in order to achieve their effect.

For decocting dryness-type formulas: combine with medicines that treat cold and thick [conditions], decocting over a vigorous fire until hot, then take; this achieves the effect of driving [the medicine] downward.

The Ru Men (Gateway of Medicine) states: for driving downward and treating cold thick medicines, these are categorized as diuretic/purgative medicines to be taken together.

For dispersing, treating wasting-thirst, and promoting diuresis: a single formula classified as a diuretic medicine should be used in large doses; if the dose is small, the medicinal power will be too weak to respond to the illness.

Depending on the illness and the nature of the medicine: for one dose, add one and a half cups of water and decocit down to one and a half cups, or at most reduce to that level.

For medicines whose character does not change: prepare properly, add one and a half cups of water per dose, and reduce to one cup, taking the whole dose at once. Depending on the condition and the individual, decoct down to one full cup.

Kindle the fire with firewood, or with well-burning charcoal, and bring it to a vigorous boil.

For medicines whose character does not change, prepare them properly with one and a half cups of water per dose.

Decoct down to eight parts [of ten] before using. For urgent illnesses, do not decoct slowly, as the medicinal strength will weaken; do not re-decoct.

For small doses, or when the patient has an acute illness, do not decoct slowly, as the medicinal power will weaken; do not decoct again.

Decoctions that have been boiled down and then cooled have good medicinal strength; the watery residue should be discarded.

One should not decoct at a low simmer, as the medicine will become thin and weak and lose its effectiveness.

As a rule, diuretic medicines should be decocted quickly so that the fresh, living energy of the just-boiling medicine is preserved.

translation:
(Right page)
When the decoction is too strong, the medicinal power is weakened if simmered too gently — this is what the Jufang Rumen (Formulary Introductions) and similar texts mean. This is the proper method for decocting medicinal preparations. Just as when brewing tea over a vigorous fire with well-burning charcoal: if you quickly bring it to a boil and drink it promptly, the fragrance and flavor are strong; but if you decoct it too long over a fierce fire, the qi of the tea weakens and the fragrance and taste deteriorate — medicines are the same.

Among common folk there is a practice called "shaking medicine": they place the medicinal herbs loosely in the pot with a small amount of water, cover it, shake it over boiling water, and when the medicinal liquid emerges, drink it quickly. By doing this at the moment the essential qi of the medicine first emerges and is most vital, it is effective for urgent conditions such as wind-cold, cholera-like disorders, abdominal pain, and food injury. However, this method is not to be used as the standard way of decocting medicines.

The correct method is simply as described above: decoct over a fierce fire quickly and then use the preparation. For formulas in the category of dispersing and resolving — such as Huoxiang Zhengqi San, Baidu San, Xiangsu San, Shensu Yin, Pingwei San, and similar dispersing preparations — decoct in this manner.

For tonifying formulas, the dosage should be adjusted: large doses should be used for deficiency of the heart and abdomen. If there is stagnation and obstruction, one dose should use two cups of water reduced to one cup. Simmer gently from the start with the medicinal herbs placed in the water, simmer slowly, then add one cup of water to the dregs and reduce to half a cup.

(Left page)
For tonifying formulas, adjust to small or large doses according to the condition of the heart and abdomen. If there is no benefit from the remainder, use two cups of water per dose reduced to one cup. If stagnation and blockage yield no benefit, use one cup of water per dose. Simmer gently, then add one cup of water to the dregs and reduce to half a cup.

Yamato Honzo, Volume 2

Combine with the first decoction, take three together on an empty stomach in the morning. When decocting tonifying medicines, boil them gently. The method for decocting tonifying medicines: Tonifying medicines should be taken in small doses; if the medicinal liquid is too dilute, the tonic medicine will be harmful rather than beneficial.

For formulas such as Buzhong Yiqi Tang, one may use wine. When fatigued and wishing to use large doses of medicine, if one adds a little stir-fried [ingredient] in this manner, it will not cause obstruction and will increase the benefit. When using Chaihu (bupleurum) with large-dose medicines, adding a small amount and stir-frying it is an old method for dispersing heat. When using Rougui (cinnamon bark) with large-dose medicines, adding a small amount is an ancient practitioner's method for addressing heat.

When a tonic medicine becomes sluggish and stagnant, use a small excess of fresh ginger to correct this.

When decocting medicines, use freshly drawn water and copper pots are acceptable. Also, when decocting medicines, silver vessels may be used, or copper pots are acceptable. Copper may impart its qi easily, so use a silver pot; measure the full capacity of white water within it, and check whether there is sediment or impurity. The size of the vessel should be such that it can hold the water. A weight of fifty units capacity is appropriate; larger than this and the medicinal liquid becomes too dilute; smaller than this and the medicinal potency will not be fully extracted.

For tonic formulas, add one slice of ginger per packet, each slice weighing two fen. For dispersing formulas, add two slices per packet, same weight as above. In both cases the skin may be included. Do not use only the skin when making decoctions; use them warm and hot.

Jing Yue [the physician] said: When taking a soup decoction with honey, bring it to a small boil so it is easy to swallow; nowadays one swallows the decoction directly. Jujubes (dates): when fresh they are large; take them when they have ripened red, and afterwards...

translation:
Steam the medicine and then dry it for use. Once dried, do not use the outer husk. When adding it to medicines, remove the pit of the jujube (大棗), and use half of one jujube per dose. Do not add too many of the remaining ones, as they will impede the action of the medicine and obstruct the flow for patients with stagnation — use six jujubes in that case, but remove them afterward.

When decocting tonic medicines (補薬), use a large amount of water. At first, boil over a strong flame (武火), and once it rises to a boil, reduce the amount of liquid; then simmer over a gentle flame (文火) for a long time, reducing it down until the decoction is well-cooked and the liquid is reduced. Drink it in small quantities. If you drink too much at once, it will stagnate and become harmful. For medicines that disperse and promote digestion (發散消導), you must not simmer them for a long time. Decoct them quickly to preserve the strong, fresh qualities of the herbs, in order to expel the pathogenic influences.

If the volume of medicinal liquid is large and taken in large doses, there will be insufficient force to drive out the pathogenic influences. Tonic medicines should be taken in small amounts but frequently, so that their effect accumulates.

Promoting-flow medicines (利湯) should be taken quickly and without prolonged use — they must not be taken for a long time. Taking diuretic/purgative preparations repeatedly and frequently is how their effect is obtained.

The book Benzhou Tongxuan states: For lower-warmer (下焦) medicines, pills should be large and hard; for middle-warmer (中焦) medicines, pills should be small and fine like steamed rice gruel-paste, so that digestion is slow. For decoction-cake thin-paste preparations, a faster digestion is intended. Water-dropped pills are even easier to digest. Honey-refined pills are intended for slow digestion.

Upon examining this: "藜" (li) does not bind into a paste; it is described as fragile and easily crumbled — what is commonly called "sakuranito" (サクナリト) is similar in nature.

It is also said: To decoct medicine dregs each time anew is by no means the ancient method. The flavor has its thick and thin aspects, the qi has its heavy and light aspects; if one takes [only part of it]...

When decocted a second time, those that are thick and heavy still retain their medicinal potency, while those that are thin and light are already exhausted of their essence. Where then is the proper balance among the principal, ministerial, assistant, and guide constituents?

Medical texts say that pills are to be made as large as a pellet (彈丸). The collected commentaries on loquat (枇杷) in the Bencao cite Su Song saying: "The loquat fruit is as large as a pellet." A pellet is a device for shooting birds — it is made of metal or fired clay, the kind of thing children play with, similar to a small iron-cannon ball.

Now in our country, the collected commentaries record Li Shizhen saying: "The loquat bears fruit as large as a pellet." Taking these two objects as the standard for the size of a pill — for example, trichosanthes seed (栝桐子): the preface and tables of the Jitong give the standard of one large bean (大豆) as the measure, saying it is about that size. "The size of trichosanthes seed" means, according to the preface and tables, six peppercorns — "as large as pepper" is the explicit statement. However, in Japan, a large bean (大豆) is considerably larger than a peppercorn, so "one large bean" is too large to serve as a proper standard. Regarding "the size of a chicken-head seed (鷄頭子)": one must know the other names for this fruit — the chicken-head plant is so called because the shape of its fruit resembles a chicken's head. The fruit has various alternate names.

To make a fine powdered medicament into pills, one kneads it together with honey in a ratio of three parts honey. The alternate name for the euryale (芡實) seed applies similarly. For making pills from medicinal powder: use six parts refined honey to four parts water, and the remainder is kneaded with the powder. If there is too much honey, the flavor will affect the stomach.

General notes:

Wrap in hot ash below and ignite — this is what is called "gu-chao" in common parlance, the method of dry-roasting. When applying heat (炙), do not cut the medicine too small. If it is large, split it and coat it with honey or ginger juice or wine to apply evenly — this applies to such things as astragalus (ōgi/黄芪). For the method called "pao" (煨), place directly into the fire and fold to insert. For the method called "chao" (炒) with thick paper placed inside the vessel, distribute the cut medicines evenly. For the method called "bei" (煏), place the cut medicines in a flat pan. Do not let the heat be either excessive or insufficient; place charcoal fire beneath and heat — this is what is called "iru" (drying by heat). Take care that it is neither overdone nor underdone. The charcoal fire is placed below. When scorched by over-roasting (炙), the medicinal nature is destroyed. As for refined honey (煉蜜), use five gō per one kin (approx. 5 fl. oz. per pound). If the medicine is scorched by over-炙, its medicinal nature is lost. Tonifying medicines should be decocted slowly in a large amount of water until thoroughly cooked, then taken. (The above follows the processing methods of the Jufang [standard formulary].) Pills: follow the established general rules, adding supplementary intentions and blending accordingly. Tonifying medicines should be decocted slowly in a large amount of water. Purgative and downward-draining medicines should be decocted quickly in less water, while the qi is still fresh, and taken promptly. Refined honey: five gō, fifteen gō per kin.

Physicians who observe illness and compose prescriptions habitually prefer small doses — and there is good reason for this. Large doses carry great risk of harm; small doses, even if the formula is not perfectly matched to the condition, carry little risk of harm. If the formula does happen to suit the illness, even a small dose will show some effect, gradually improving the condition over time. Moreover, because physicians often lack certain insight, when facing a patient they cannot commit to a single prescription, and so they often proceed by trial, testing medicines one after another.

translation:
When one looks to see whether a formula is appropriate, if it does not address the disease one must repeatedly change the formula — this is what ordinary physicians do. Although this may seem like rough craftsmanship, it comes from being practiced and experienced in the ways of the world. When a skilled physician has a clear target, a casual observer cannot trust it so firmly.

The world has long been misled by the theories of Rotenmin, borrowing unsuitable things and carelessly using rehmannia, scrophularia, and nutmeg, combining peony and other herbs in formulations that all come into contact with copper and iron vessels, which is contrary to the precepts — and yet people ignore this and do not believe in the principle stated in the Huangdi Bencao of three hundred items, but carry on as if undisturbed, thinking themselves well-versed and dismissing the rule as eccentric.

Alas, these people do not understand that the ancients established their rules based on the physical properties of mutual control among things. One may try to explain it to the ignorant, but they act recklessly — how lamentable is this blind faith.

The character 鑪 (lu), as explained in the Zihui, refers to a wine vessel. The text says "three and eight gou, simmer in one lu" — the lu referred to here is a large wine vessel as used in China, and should be understood as a large wine vessel.

The characters 宇書 and 卻助 share the same pronunciation; 一勧郎 also. The Zihui says that nowadays the popular usage is widespread.

The preface and formulary regulations state: "a knife-spatula (dao gui) is one-tenth of a square-inch spoon (fang cun bi); use as a standard one paulownia seed's worth, scooped up without spilling."

I note: "seven" here means "to make seven," a one-cun square measure, scoop without spilling as the standard.

The Xiangdai Chunbian in twelve volumes corrects the term; the Bencao preface and formulary use the term 吹咀 (chuiju); the second character 咀 follows the mouth radical — this is also not entirely accurate as a term for preparation. This applies also to the Eastern [tradition].

It is better to finely cut [the drugs] in the manner of chuiju — "chui" referring to the method of fine preparation.

[The statement of] Yuan [Zai] about the boundaries:

Cai says: when using wine in a decoction, one must add it just as the decoction is about to finish boiling and then remove from heat. ○ [As opposed to] adding the wine from the beginning of the decoction.

Chen Zangqi says: When preparing decoctions, substances such as musk, ox bezoar, rhinoceros horn, antelope horn, cattail pollen, cinnabar, mirabilite, and donkey-hide gelatin must be ground into a fine powder and stirred into the hot liquid at the moment of serving, then drunk.

Zhen says: The ancients, when using tonifying medicines, always combined them with medicines to expel pathogens. Once the pathogen is gone, the tonic can do its work fully. This is the key principle. Later generations do not understand this, and so those who take tonics continuously will inevitably suffer from one-sided excess as a result.

The Ming Biao Za Zhu states: Whenever treating illness, one must first carefully examine whether there is food accumulation or dietary injury. One should first regulate the spleen and stomach to guide digestion, and only afterward proceed with other medical treatment. Collecting too many remedies leads to imbalance.

In Jujia Bibei it is written: Danxi relied exclusively on cooling medicines, which is also not appropriate. Moreover, in today's age, vital qi is daily depleted. Using Danxi's method, many patients develop a damaged spleen and stomach, leading to the generation of dampness-heat and vacuity-swelling. One must use Li Dongyuan's method of supplementing the spleen. Furthermore, it is said that Danxi's approach, while attentive to examining the human constitution and the origin of illness, tends to overuse bitter-cold medicines in cases of yang vacuity, causing persistent yin vacuity. While Danxi's method of supplementing yin and Li Dongyuan's method of warming and supplementing the spleen and stomach appear different, those who favor supplementing yin should be mindful of the seasonal conditions when applying the method.

translation:
On aromatic substances in medicines: measure them dry and store them.
Pass them through [a process], seal them in a jar like tea — this is how it should be done. Spices such as pepper, Japanese pepper, cardamom, white cardamom, cinnamon tube, moutan, and the like — if left over days, their aroma dissipates, their potency weakens, and grinding large amounts at once is not advisable. Cinnamon bark, cloves, and such things — even if ground to powder overnight, the flavor becomes weak.
Aromatic substances all tend to lose their fragrance and flavor.
Civet, realgar, white sandalwood, borneol camphor, dew-of-incense, pepper, perilla, mint, jasmine — all such things: if greatly disturbed, the aroma dissipates. This is the reason.
Someone says: the custom in this country is to use Mozuku [a type of seaweed] in place of false hellebore, and charcoal in place of dried lacquer. These substitutions are used in making medicines.
The old popular formulas used [such things]; they entered into use as harmonizing recipes and came to be called "harmonizing formulas." The Chinese formulas use genuine materials; it is said that there is no need to go beyond this.
Also, the "Bitan" [Brush Talks, i.e. Mengxi Bitan] has a reasonable argument: pills, powders, and decoctions each have their appropriate uses, and though in ancient formulas decoctions were not used in this way, people in recent ages have come to use them.
For reaching the five viscera and the four limbs, nothing surpasses a decoction; for remaining lodged in the middle [of the body], nothing surpasses a pill. Pills act slowly and release gradually; decoctions act quickly; powders are intermediate. For severe toxins, pills are to be used; for seeking quick action, use a decoction; for a somewhat slower effect, use a powder.

translation:
[Section heading: Discourse]

In using pills and decoctions, this is the general outline. In recent times those who use decoctions apply heat fully — all are煎 (simmered) preparations. As a rule, decoctions in liquid form are complete in vigor and force, and are several times more powerful than pills or powders. If the medicinal power is great, then a single dose need not exceed three to five qian at most — such is the advantage of their efficacy over others. One should not be constrained by fixed formulas. When the medicinal force is great, one must not let the right moment slip; the entire management of this lies in the skilled practitioner; it cannot simply be followed mechanically.

Yunlin [Gong Tingxian] compiled eight categories of medical writings; the formulas and discussions that appear repeatedly before and after one another — Chen Jiamo's treatments he incorporated into the "Yunlin Verse Compendium," extracting the medicinal nature songs, combining duplicated and redundant material into one, so that readers who study and examine the various books can remove what is superfluous, keeping what is essential. The writing is not entirely pure. The book circulated and yet it obscured the achievements of those who came before, claiming credit for itself.

What Lizhai [Xue Ji] compiled for his own amusement, though it was the work of a cultivated gentleman — such writings, even if not without merit, are yet indulgent, each sweeping moral principle aside; their intellectual orientation is base. Vulgar habits, fixed on imitation, take pleasure in what is unseemly, and this is the private art of a self-serving craftsman. How low and mean is such a practice! And yet, because these works were used by practicing physicians for dispensing medicines, assembling prescriptions most suited to the climate of the later Ming period, they are appropriate to the climate and soil of our country; even for slight and weak ailments — ah, how one like Yanchuan [Gong Tingxian] in his learning and insight, though not equal to the ancients, was a master hand of later generations. What he wrote may be trusted.

It is essential to understand that the method of cultivating health in this world lies in accumulating virtue. Those who study medicine in order to sustain life will naturally become celebrated physicians, held in esteem by lords and nobles. Those who make this art a household practice will naturally gain both fame and profit — it is commonly seen that being a celebrated physician ranks first. If one masters the art of preserving life, the benefits will serve one's whole body for ten years and never be exhausted.

translation:
Reading books without mastering them is like studying medicine without achieving proficiency. The ancients said: to practice medicine is to learn it properly. Becoming a doctor merely for the sake of common people, while not following the correct methods, is truly not the right way — as this saying makes clear.

Good physicians are rare, and therefore the physician holds the people's lives in hand; life itself depends on medicine. It is a weighty responsibility. One must carefully choose the right person for it — someone of clear understanding and sound reasoning. A person who lacks knowledge must not be made a physician. To make an ignorant person a physician is to write people off as lost. Even heaven's way suggests that those who would be parents to others must choose a good physician, so that the people's illnesses may be properly treated. One must not allow common people, as one's own children, to be harmed by mediocre doctors.

Those who practice medicine must read widely and deeply, mastering the principles of yin-yang and the five phases as they apply to the human body and all things. Only then can one truly understand. Without this, the understanding of illness will be imprecise. Just as in writing there is the orthodox and the unorthodox, so too in the medical arts there is the right and wrong path. One must select and apply the correct methods.

Those who are merely clever craftsmen in their approach use the art of medicine without truly grasping its reasoning. No one who has not read books has ever become a good physician. Even if someone has some learning, without studying the foundational texts, they are like someone who claims to be skilled at poetry without having studied the rules of verse. To practice medicine without reading is to proceed without understanding its principles.

Those who rely on crude, hand-me-down techniques become numerous, and thinking this sufficient, they neglect to study the classical Chinese medical texts. Without studying broadly, one cannot be a true physician. Only one who has studied thoroughly and can explain medicine with clarity is a worthy and praiseworthy physician — one who may truly be trusted and employed for the benefit of the people.

Medicine is a civil art; though one may be naturally untalented, those born with good fortune will, when the time comes, be employed by those in the world. If the person employing the physician has no literary learning, the physician cannot truly excel. It is only when one's own spirit is in accord with the age that one is reckoned a skilled craftsman. Therefore, those not naturally gifted must seek instruction from many people, diligently polish their art and technique, and so become a good physician.

Among those of good family and low birth alike, many intelligent young students come seeking guidance. If one reads the medical classics devotedly for ten years, one will surely become a good physician. Once one has studied under a good master and devoted many years to perfecting one's skills in medicine, one will naturally come to understand its principles.

Name, profit, and a good reputation will come of themselves; to seek them deliberately is like trying to pick up something lying right before you. Even a man of humble and poor station, by mastering his craft and understanding how to nurture life, bringing long life to himself and relief to others, and combining these benefits — fame, profit, and a good reputation will come to him naturally without difficulty.

Section One

Kikkyū (Podophyllum): alternate name. ○ Hemp seed (火麻仁): according to the Bencao, this is cannabis (大麻), not sesame (胡麻). ○ Yong fish: similarly noted. ○ The foregoing entries give only a general listing of names; full details cannot be exhaustively covered here—see corresponding entries.

Drugs mistakenly used in Japan in place of the correct ones: ○ Rénshēn (ginseng): the physician Ma Xin says that contemporary doctors substitute ginseng with qí nǐ (Adenophora), platycodon root, and lu-fang-kui-jie rénshēn, or those with a bitter taste—yet these are all different in nature and flavor and are not of the same type. Some are thinning and drain dampness; these harmful substitutes cannot truly replace ginseng. If a substitute must be used out of necessity, sha shen (Adenophora stricta) or ru gen may serve, since they do not harm the patient. Though a single ingredient of light character cannot raise the dead, if used in sufficient quantity some small benefit may accrue. To use the ancient method of substituting sha shen for ginseng has true merit—it has a flavor among the five tastes and can consolidate and astringe. However, the domestic Japanese variety has only a bitter taste among the five, and one fears it lacks the supplementing and consolidating action; rather, it promotes drainage and free flow, which is a concern. Do not use it. ○ Sha shen: it is appropriate to use [the correct variety].

Tōsho-shun: details regarding the root described in the Bencao and its Japanese equivalents are given in the relevant entry. ○ Regarding Chinese mugwort (外麻): the popular identification does not match; do not use—see the relevant entry for details. ○ Bupleurum (柴胡): what is described in the Bencao differs somewhat from the Japanese; the Kamakura variety may be used. ○ The Chinese-imported cultivated variety: there are two kinds, neither of which is genuine; preparation at home according to proper method is acceptable, but the commercially sold pharmacy version should not be trusted. ○ Do not use the Chinese-imported processed form; use only the genuine article imported directly from China. ○ Zhǐ shí and zhǐ ké (unripe and ripe bitter orange): do not use [the Japanese substitutes]. ○ Wáng guā (王瓜): that which is called tama-kazura in Japan is this plant. translation:
Right page (Lun):

There are two kinds that resemble Gualou (trichosanthes) but are not it; these are coarse, inferior things and should not be collected for use. They are described below under their respective entries. Huhuanglian (Picrorrhiza): The common custom has long mistakenly used the herb "Senburi" (Swertia japonica), but one must use the true Chinese variety. Baibu (Stemona): What the common custom has long called Baibu is not the genuine article; what it actually is remains uncertain. Gouji (Cibotium): In recent years the fresh root from China has arrived; the common custom of using bitter fern is incorrect. Sharen (cardamom): The common custom of using purple fern for it is wrong. The root used is said to be good, but millet-yellow substitutes are not correct. The common custom is wrong; using the Izu stone-fruit (a local substitute) for it is also incorrect. Zhizi (gardenia fruit), Baihe (lily): Using tea substitutes is wrong; the white-flowered variety should be used. Shanyao (Chinese yam): those grown in garden plots may also be used. One must use the mountain-grown variety; those from mountain gardens harvested in the appropriate month are acceptable — the intent should be self-evident. Garden-grown ones may also be used, but difficult substitutes should not be employed.

Left page (Pu):

Minguo (an herb): What is called by this name here is not the true herb; the Bencao states that Minguo's qi, though it resembles what in Japan is called Guanghuo, differs in whether its qi is truly robust. Qingpi and Chenpi (citrus peels): Only those coming from China are of good quality and may be used. Zhusha (cinnabar): The Chensha from Shizhou; some use it. Those coming directly from China are superior. Coarse craftsmen who use limestone are wrong. Baixianpi (dictamnus bark): Chinese imports are superior. Those who use magnolia bark as a substitute are wrong. Dafengzi (chaulmoogra): Using Leiwan (a fungus) for it is wrong; those coming from China may be used. Baixianpi: using wood-mallet bark as a substitute is wrong. Even if it comes from China, if it lacks fragrance it should not be long used as a medicinal substitute. As for Xiangru (elsholtzia): those with a fragrant aroma and pungent taste may be used as medicinal substitutes. Those with a foul odor and no fragrance should not be used. What is called "ryuno-hakka" (dragon-brain mint), like peppermint, is acceptable to call by that name, but calling it by the name associated with foul odor is incorrect.

或負其小康而不慎節呑此忽受傷害頓残生命者往
往有之是以大率衰老之人受病而致死者因傷
translation:
Thin sake lees are not suitable. As for honey: druggists frequently make counterfeits using sugar, so one must not use these. One should select and obtain honey sold by those who come from mountain villages. Tokushin says: The above reflects common practice in this country. Most of what remains has lost its true quality — one fears that people simply follow established custom without question.

One must never carelessly use medicines without carefully selecting them. When it comes to medicines, careful discernment is essential. Those who are not thorough in this may find their lives endangered. One must not carelessly use medicines; the selection of them requires great care and attentiveness. Those who are mired in old habits may follow a method of selection, yet if they cling rigidly to it without flexibility, they may be called faithful to their diet and yet still lack true discernment.

On the matter of regulating food and drink for nurturing life: there are many arts and techniques, but one should look to the broad picture and regulate one's eating and drinking accordingly. In general, what is beneficial is fresh, fragrant, and clean food. One must inevitably make choices about what to take and what to discard. As a rule, things that nourish and replenish the person should be chosen; things that harm the person should be set aside. Tokushin privately considers: in the way of food and drink, though it is said to be difficult to present a single standard for all people, regulation is essential.

Foods that are raw and cold, or hot and scorched, fatty, rich, hard, or greasy all overtax the intestines and stomach and cannot be recommended. Foods that are gently warm, tender, mild in flavor, and moderate in nature are all able to benefit a person and may be praised. Foods in which the five flavors are unbalanced, or whose nature is harsh and intense, are harmful to the intestines and stomach and cannot easily be tolerated.

In the case of the greatly aged and elderly, their diet commonly tends to stagnate and is difficult to reform. They suffer many injuries. It is most important to prohibit these harmful foods. If such indulgence was not restrained even in the prime of life, or if one grows lax on account of feeling temporarily well and fails to regulate one's eating, one may suddenly suffer injury and damage to life — this happens frequently. Thus, in most cases, the deaths of the elderly from illness are caused by dietary injury.

text:

腸脾胃柿林栁胡瓜等生果不可食蒸熱ハ味ヨク又不
「蒸熱ニ熱キヲ食ス也性熱ナル湯ニ共ニ生ヲ久ク熟ルヨリコシ」
凡老人虛人ハ蘿蔔松茸葡萄菜竹筍加牛蒡卷丹胡羅蔔芋等

「豆油ニテヨク腑胃虛者熟ノハ一切ノ生菜菜根ヲ生氣ナン或淡米消又
腸胃ヲ傷ルス也滷ニ患ナン古語ニ以胃熱ニタルヲモテ生物ハ胃熟後食」
ナイヘルガ如クス也滷ニ患ナン古語ニ以腑胃熟後ニ生菜不可多食宜シ
或日無病人ハ生菜易消化鹽藏及者肉飼消難消化無生氣者
今試亦然盖有生氣者素軟而易消化無生氣者
translation:
When it comes to food and drink, in eight or nine cases out of ten one may avoid harm — is this not so?

Elderly people and those with weak spleen and stomach must absolutely avoid all raw, cold, hard, tough, oily, rich, and sticky foods. Raw fish should not be eaten by sick people; salted and astringent things should be steamed for one or two days before consumption, as this fully develops the qi and improves the flavor — steamed fish is better than simply boiled. Steamed and well-cooked foods are good; anything still raw must not be eaten. Steaming until fully cooked is best for flavor and for the nature of the food. Sea cucumber, birds, and beasts: first wash their innards once in rice-washing water, steam them thoroughly, and then the next day boil them again. Vegetables should likewise be cut into three-to-seven sections, and root vegetables too should be treated in the same way — steamed fully, the flavor will be excellent and they will not damage the intestines. Persimmons, chestnuts, willow-cucumbers, and other raw fruits must not be eaten; when steamed they taste better and cause no harm. [Note: It is best to eat things hot from steaming; a preparation steeped in hot water with other ingredients and cooked through is superior to merely boiling raw things for a long time.]

In general, for elderly or weak persons, daikon radish, matsutake mushroom, grape, greens, bamboo shoot, burdock root, carrot, taro, and similar things — all may be steamed and eaten. Their qi and flavor are not harmful; a light rice-water preparation also soothes the stomach. [Note: Using bean oil to cook them well is good for those with weak stomach; all raw vegetables and root vegetables contain raw qi; a light rice preparation also protects the intestines and stomach. Damaging the stomach with brine is a risk. The old saying goes: after the stomach is warmed, raw foods should be eaten only after cooking.] Just as harmful fluids can injure one, the old saying holds: one should not eat too many raw greens after the stomach and bowels have been warmed; it is better to eat them after the stomach is fully warmed.

As for people in ordinary good health: raw vegetables are easy to digest; salted or preserved or boiled meat is difficult to digest and lacks living qi. Testing this, one finds it is indeed so: foods that retain living qi are naturally soft and easy to digest, while those without living qi are not.

法
李筌翁曰論蔬食之美者日清日紫日芸覆日鬆腓
而已又日至美之物皆利于狐行　言ハ菜ノ可食、

類ナリ潔トハ人カニテ潔クスル也園菜水草果蔬モ
translation:
[Hard and difficult to digest.]

I, Ekiken, have long heard it said that the blood and vital energy of humans and the six domesticated animals are comparable, and that meat can supplement and nourish the human body. This reasoning is sound in principle, and since ancient times it has been said that meat replenishes people. However, considering the different climates and soils of China and the various lands, and the different constitutions with which people are endowed, there are things that are suitable and things that are not suitable for each person. In China, people are constituted to benefit from such foods, but Japanese people are not so constituted — their nature tends to be delicate and weak. The flavors of the six domestic animals are rich and strong, and therefore Japanese people cannot well receive such flavors. They do not eat or offer in ritual the meat of cattle, horses, or large sheep. They subsist on vegetables, fish, fowl, and shellfish — things of mild and light flavor. The elderly especially have weakened digestive function, and it is proper to nourish the body with these foods, following the requirements of one's climate and soil. For the elderly, raw meat should be used sparingly; it is better to use boiled, steamed, or lightly broiled dishes with thin sauces. Fish and fowl preserved by drying or salting should be eaten only rarely, three times in a hundred, as it were. Oily preserved foods should not be eaten. Rich and fatty foods should not be eaten in excess. People of certain foreign countries, when starving, eat human flesh and consume the six domesticated animals indiscriminately. People of our country are different in this respect, because the climate and soil differ, and accordingly people's tastes and what is suitable for them also differ. Because people's constitutions and the climate differ, their tastes and what suits them change accordingly.

Method:
Master Li Quan, in his discussion of the excellence of vegetable foods, said: "The finest are the clear, the purple, the aromatic, and the light." That is all. He also said that the finest of all things benefit those who travel nimbly. By "clear" he means vegetables that are naturally clean and pure — mountain greens, water plants, and garden produce of this kind. By "pure" he means things made clean through human effort — garden vegetables, water plants, and fruits and vegetables alike.

毎食訖以手摩面及腹令津液通流飲食當行步蹋
踏計使中數里来飲食即卧乃生百病飲食飭節卧
translation:
Water — soak well in rope-water for two or three days, wash thoroughly, and tie off the ends. What is called "fragrant and aromatic" (芳馥) refers to a pleasant scent; what is called "soft and tender" (髣脆) refers to something soft. These four qualities are what is fitting to eat; they are all things that please the spleen and stomach.
Foods of outstanding flavor should not be mixed with other ingredients but boiled alone — bamboo shoots and pine mushrooms are of this type. These things, which the Japanese by nature enjoy, may serve as a pleasure and a medicine.
Foods that one has a natural liking for do not cause harm; on the contrary, they become medicine. However, if one eats and drinks them to excess, they invariably cause harm.

In his later years, Zhu Xi personally wrote one notice warning his children, saying: "For years now my inner illness has been largely due to excess in eating and drinking." After the age of sixty-eight, rice with meat at morning and evening meals repeatedly caused harm; one must never exceed one portion of meat. Zhu Xi further said: Do not add further meat dishes; at the evening meal eat even less. As for drinking wine, stopping at half-intoxication is the proper measure. This is what Zhu Xi wrote to his children warning against excess in food and drink — one portion of meat at morning and evening, even less at the evening meal, and stopping wine at the halfway point. This advice on both meat dishes and plain food is most pertinent and apt.
Tang Gao Shilang's brothers ate no more than two side dishes; in the evening they ate little and simply stored their gourd vessels — they did not overindulge.

These several sayings are all worth following as rules for moderating food and drink; living in this way is how one preserves the full span of one's years. This is the Way.

After each meal, rub the face and abdomen with the hands so that the fluids and humors circulate freely. After eating one should walk, covering a distance of several li. Going straight to bed after eating gives rise to a hundred illnesses. Regulate food and drink, and then rest.

translation:
On Relieving Abdominal Distension: A Thousand Gold Remedies

The Medical Discourses say: When one eats a great variety of foods and feels the body growing tired and sluggish, one should not immediately lie down to sleep. Instead, walk slowly for a hundred or more steps, then loosen the sash and clothing, stretch the waist, sit upright, and use both hands to massage the chest and abdomen, moving them back and forth some dozens of times, so that the qi passages of the chest and abdomen do not become blocked from overeating. Pressing and rubbing several dozen times with both hands along the flanks aids digestion.

Song dynasty Cheng Zhengmin said: In ancient times, elders after meals would invariably take a stroll, wishing to move the body so as to aid digestion. This is why later people took up the practice of strolling after meals. — from Picking Orchids: Miscellaneous Notes

Su Dongpo said: After every meal he would rinse his mouth with strong tea, and the greasiness and coating would be dispelled, leaving the stomach clean. Whatever meat remained between the teeth would, under the astringent bitterness of the tea, naturally be dislodged; there was no need to pick and probe with a toothpick.

Xu Luqi said: The elderly should eat foods refined by cooking and should not eat too much coarse grain, for this benefits those whose qi is weak and who cannot tolerate gruel. That is the reason.

Donggu once remarked: The human body is rooted in the spleen and stomach. Now the spleen and stomach have their preferences and dislikes — they favor warmth and dislike cold, favor dryness and dislike dampness, favor sweetness and dislike bitterness, favor cleanliness and dislike hidden filth, favor soft and delicate foods and dislike hard ones, favor fresh foods and dislike stale and rotten ones, favor refined and rich foods and dislike coarse ones. If one can follow what the spleen and stomach favor and keep away from what they dislike, the spleen and stomach will remain harmonious and balanced, and illness will be rare.

The Expanded Monthly Compendium says: The viscera and bowels delight in what is fragrant and clean, and are harmed when the spleen and stomach lose their harmony.

達生録曰飲食須用煖盆養脾胃喜溫不以冷熱記又日尤忌生冷硬物寿養叢書日夏月伏陰在内煖食尤宜

天之生人水穀以養之水之滋養者過半夫人之形
translation:
The Tassho-roku states: "When eating and drinking, one should use warm vessels to nourish the spleen and stomach, which rejoice in warmth. Do not use things that are cold or hot indiscriminately." It also says: "Above all, avoid raw, cold, and hard foods." The Juyo Sosho states: "In the summer months, yin is hidden within, so it is especially appropriate to eat warm food."

The spleen and stomach are the foundation of the body's vitality and growth. Therefore, the way to preserve one's health lies in being careful and moderate in eating and drinking, and in cultivating the spleen and stomach. The way of careful moderation has patience as its key virtue. The classics say: "The greatest transgressions inevitably arise from a momentary failure of patience — preserve your body whole." An ancient poem says: "Patience surpasses great obstacles." This is what it means to practice the way of patience. The principle of patience is actually quite straightforward: it is a matter of mastering the mind and suppressing anger. How great is the meaning of patience! The method of restraining the body lies in the practice of patience. If one has no texts beyond this to guide one, one must always obtain guidance and apply effort. At the moment of eating — three mouthfuls — if one practices careful patience, then eating becomes just one practice. And yet, to be able to endure this and overcome anger is the method. And yet the reason people cannot endure is that they are driven by a single point of appetite — hence what is most difficult becomes, oddly, what feels easy. The same applies below.

Dietary therapy is also a matter of the utmost immediacy and importance and must not be overlooked in nourishing oneself. One should first use dietary therapy and only afterward resort to medicinal treatments. For the elderly, dietary therapy methods for maintaining health are most appropriate; one should then turn to medicinal prescriptions. There are many such instances where the elderly rely on dietary therapy. One should select and use this method. Among the many medical texts past and present — the Yoro Shincho, the Igaku Nyumon, the Kyoka Hitsuyo, and others — all contain sections on dietary therapy.

The Yoro Shincho, the Igaku Nyumon, the Kyoka Hitsuyo, and others all contain dietary prescriptions worth consulting.

Heaven gave birth to humans and sustains them with grain and water. More than half of what nourishes the human form comes from water.

translation:
Right page (read right to left, top to bottom):

The body has thick and thin constitutions, the vital energy has clear and turbid qualities, the stomach and intestines have strong and weak states, and age has long and short spans. Much of this depends on the quality of the local water and soil. Is not water not also critically important to people? One must not fail to select good water and use it.

Among plants, birds, beasts, insects, and fish, there are poisonous things. One must know them in advance and not eat them. Even if something appears delicious, if its nature has not been tested, one cannot know whether it is poisonous or not.

Tao Zhen-ren's song on eating says: "Eat slowly and steadily; after eating, walk a hundred steps, rub both hands along the sides and over the belly and abdomen; bend and turn the body, massaging the kidney region — this is called moving water and earth, facing upward and exhaling 'ha'." Exhale three or four times; naturally the toxic qi from food will dissipate. This is considered the proper method for those who cultivate themselves, and should be practiced daily.

The Five Grains:
Millet (禾), barnyard millet (稗), foxtail millet (粟), wheat (麦), beans (豆). The Su Wen, "Treatise on the Seasonal Regulation of Visceral Qi," states: "The five grains nourish, the five domestic animals benefit, the five fruits assist." The Monthly Ordinances lists: glutinous millet, panicled millet, hemp, and beans as the five grains. The Chu Ci commentary gives: rice, panicled millet, wheat, beans, and hemp as the five grains.

The Five Domestic Animals: chicken, sheep, ox, horse, pig (with the addition of the dog making six domestic animals for household keeping).

Students of natural studies should memorize and recite this; here is a summary. The diseases of the limbs and body are numerous.

Rice, soybeans, adzuki beans, barley, wheat, millet, barnyard millet, hemp, and pearl millet. [Circle mark]

One: Rice varieties are numerous; large and small beans, large and small wheat — as annotated by Zheng Xuan in the Zhou Rites.
The Nine Grains: [associated with] wood/bitter, fire/sweet, earth/pungent, metal/salty, water.
The Five Flavors: cold, hot, warm, cool, salty/metal/water.
The Four Qi: [wind causing] miasma belongs to the liver; the raw smell of autumn is fragrant; earth's scorched smell belongs to summer's decay — as recorded in the Monthly Ordinances.
The Five Odors: The rancid smell of spring, the raw smell of autumn, the scorched smell belonging to earth, the decaying smell of summer — as recorded in the Monthly Ordinances. This pertains to the nature of medicines.
The Five Entries [into the organs]: Zhang Yuansu said: sour enters the liver, bitter enters the heart, sweet enters the spleen, pungent enters the lungs, salty enters the kidneys. The lungs smell like chicken, fish, and duck larvae; the kidneys smell like asafoetida sweat and fragrant musk; [other organs smell] like aloeswood, sandalwood, and dragon [incense].

The Seven Relationships of Medicines: A medicine acting alone — Li Shizhen says a single-ingredient formula does not need a complementary substance. Mutually requiring substances belong to the same category and cannot be separated. A guiding substance acts as an assistant and guide. Mutually antagonistic substances are incompatible with each other. [Some combinations produce] toxicity. The ancients frequently used mutually opposing combinations that cause harm, but there are also substances that counteract such harm, and these are recorded for the understanding of practitioners. Zong Ye said: mutually opposing substances cause more harm than those that are merely counteractive. The above is taken from the Bencao. My own view: among the seven relationships, mutually antagonistic combinations are commonly used but can be harmful and should not be used routinely; the remaining five types are harmless when used and are the ones commonly employed.

Supplement

Yamato Honzo, Volume [18]

Three Categories of Plants and Trees: The "Invisible Immortal's Secret" (Wuzheng Shen Yin) says that the varieties of plants and trees are extremely numerous and varied; broadly speaking there are three kinds: woody plants (trees), vine plants, and herbaceous plants.

Seven Treasures: Gold — yellow gold, white silver, red copper, black iron, blue tin; Silver; Lapis lazuli; Agate; Glass; Pearl; Coral.

Five Pungents: The term comes from Buddhist scripture; also called the Five Rank Vegetables. According to the Bencao (Materia Medica), Lu Shan — the physician Zhen says their pungent smell drives away spirits and demons. Used to ward off pestilent airs; the category includes: Chinese chives, garlic, shallots, and scallions. These are consumed on the seventh day of the first month as the Seven Herb Gruel, based on their intrinsic properties.

The Seven Herbs of Human Day: The Jingchu Suishi Ji (Record of Annual Rites of Jing and Chu) makes no mention of "seven varieties" by name. In popular custom, on Human Day (the seventh day of the first month) a gruel is made. Now, consulting the Suishi Ji: on the seventh day of the first month, seven kinds of vegetables are used.

The seven varieties called the "Seven Herbs" are:
1. Seri (water parsley / Oenanthe javanica)
2. Nazuna (shepherd's purse)
3. Gogyo (cudweed) — also called "Buddha's ear grass." [Note: Some people mistakenly identify this with yellow-flowered artemisia, but that is incorrect.]
4. Hotokenoza (henbit) — also called Tazako; a kind of Brassica/mustard green, with spreading vines. Also called "Buddha's seat." Also called田平子 (field-flat-plant), a type of green vegetable. In popular usage it is called Suzuna; the variety found growing in paddies is called "floating suzuna," while the dry-field variety is called "畠公事菘" (field-service turnip). Its root resembles what is described in the Kyona entry — namely daikon (large radish). These are the seven varieties. [Note: Regarding the suzuna entry, the畠公事 variety's root resembles shallot / shepherd's purse.]

Birth Periods by Month [of various creatures]: Humans gestate ten months; horses twelve months; dogs three to four months; [monkeys] five months; deer six months; tigers seven months; insects eight months. (Source: Kongzi Jiayu — Sayings of Confucius's School.)

Chinese Weights and Measures: One zi = two fen and a half; one tie = four fen; one qian = [ten units], equivalent to the same [as above].

translation:
Choosing a physician poorly and not recognizing the nature of an illness: the eight failures. When even one is present, it is called "difficult to treat." (Same as above.)

Five Movements (Wu Yun): The movements of the Five Phases. Six Qi: Wind-Wood, Minister Fire. The four qi of Heaven are: Wind, Cold, Summer-heat, Dampness, Dryness, and Metal.

Seven Emotions: Cold, Fire, Minister Fire.

(Section on the emotions): Joy, Anger, Sorrow, Pleasure, Love, Hatred, Desire — as recorded in body records. Joy, Anger, Worry, Pensiveness, Grief, Fear, Fright.

Five Wills: Joy, Anger, Pensiveness, Worry, Fear — from the Hidden Texts.

Eight Pathogens: Wind, Cold, Summer-heat, and Dampness are external pathogens. Eating, drinking, taxation, and indolence are internal pathogens.

Five Pathogenic Factors: Wind, Summer-heat, Cold, Dampness, Dryness.

Six conditions under which treatment is difficult (from the Shiji): (1) When wealth is valued more than health; (2) when clothing and food are inappropriate; (3) when the yin-yang and organ qi are unsettled; (4) when not reasoned through properly; (5) when one trusts shamans over physicians; (6) when the body is already wasted and cannot take medicine. When even one of these six applies, treatment is difficult.

Five Flavors encompassing the Five Organs: The Qianjin Fang states that the five flavors should not be taken in excess or partial abundance. Thus: excessive sour damages the spleen; excessive bitter damages the five organs — this is the natural principle of the Five Phases.

Five Taxations (Wu Lao): The heart dislikes fence (palisade/constriction), the vessels dislike cold, the liver dislikes wind, the spleen dislikes dampness, the kidneys dislike dryness. The Qianjin Fang states: those who are good at nurturing life constantly keep to: less pensiveness, less grief, less pleasure, less joy, less anger.

Five Aversions (Wu E): Walking injures the sinews; prolonged looking injures the blood; prolonged lying injures the qi; prolonged sitting injures the flesh; prolonged standing injures the bones.

On Nurturing Life — Twelve Fires: The heart dislikes constriction, the vessels dislike cold, the liver dislikes wind, the bowels dislike dampness, the kidneys dislike dryness. The Qianjin Fang states: those skilled at nurturing life constantly practice: less pensiveness, less grief, less pleasure, less joy, less anger, less talking, less business, less eating, less worry, less sorrow, less moving about, less hatred.

translation:
Yamato Honzo, Volume One

To practice these twelve [precepts] is the essential key to nurturing one's nature. Excessive thinking injures the spirit — and so it is said.
If these twelve [harmful excesses] are not eliminated, then the protective vital forces will lose their proper measure, and this becomes the root of a ruined life. It is sincerely affirmed that human affairs are manifold and countless; human desires follow along with them, and this is what destroys life. These things pertain to practical matters. The measures [of desire] are habitually excessive and go beyond the mean; one must reduce and moderate them. That is what the writings mean by "hitting the mean." Sun Simiao spoke of these twelve points as a general outline, nothing more. But in reality, it is not merely these twelve — broadly speaking, all affairs require careful attention. This is the way to a long and lasting life.
